Could your brain data be used against you? UN calls for limits on neurotechnology

Brain signals recorded by a gaming headset or a wellness gadget could one day be used as evidence against you in court, according to a new UN report which warns that neurotechnology is outpacing the laws meant to protect human rights.

Presenting the Secretary-General’s report to the General Assembly on Thursday, senior human rights official Claudia Fuentes Julio said the technology could threaten privacy, freedom of thought and the right to a fair trial, particularly for marginalised people.
- The new report examines the growing use of neurotechnology in justice systems and the risks arising from its convergence with artificial intelligence (AI)
- Data collected through gaming or wellness devices, for instance, could be used in a court of law, impacting fundamental human rights, including the right to a fair trial
- The report calls for prohibiting coercive and abusive applications of neurotechnology and establishing stronger legal and ethical safeguards
Neurotechnology was once exclusively used for medical diagnoses or treatment, measuring, monitoring, analysing, predicting or modulating the nervous system.
The new tech gathers neural data – defined as qualitative and quantitative data about the structure, activity and function of the nervous system.

“Neurotechnology accesses, measures and analyses brain signals,” the UN chief wrote in his report. “If these signals are treated as direct indicators of thoughts, intentions or truthfulness, the use of neural data points could undermine how we understand and value each of us as human beings.”

Once confined to clinical or research environments, these devices are now entering, or may enter, consumer markets, workplaces, schools, public services, law enforcement and justice systems, the report found.

UN Assistant Secretary-General for Human Rights Claudia Fuentes Julio highlighted a range of risks when introducing the report to Third Committee members, including the growing commercialisation of neurotechnology and the collection of large volumes of neural data by technology companies.
Marketed for wellness, gaming and productivity, wearable, so-called electroencephalography devices are now increasingly available.

As such, neural data collected through these devices could be accessed by governments or introduced as evidence in legal proceedings without adequate recognition of its highly sensitive nature, the report warned.

While these new technologies hold significant promise, particularly for medical and assistive applications, Ms. Fuentes Julio said the report “warns of risks to dignity, privacy, freedom of thought, fair trial rights, liberty and protection from ill-treatment, especially for marginalised groups”.

Indeed, when applied in the courtroom these technologies serve different purposes and pose distinct legal and human rights risks, especially as tools and data developed for medical use are repurposed without appropriate safeguards, the report argues.

Ms. Fuentes Julio said the report calls for “prohibitions on coercive and abusive uses, and stronger safeguards, informed consent, scientific validation, oversight, accountability and protection of neural data.”
The report emphasises that neural data, as “uniquely sensitive personal data,” demands heightened protection.
The world is waging a ‘war on nature’ as progress on biodiversity targets lags

Fewer than half of the national targets set to protect the world’s plants, animals and ecosystems are on track, the UN warns in a new report, days before countries gather in Yerevan, Armenia, for the COP17 biodiversity conference.
The landmark deal struck in Montreal in 2022 – the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework – set out a vision of “living in harmony with nature” by 2050, with urgent action needed by 2030.
The new report suggests the world is falling behind.

“Biodiversity underpins life on Earth,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres wrote in the report. “Safeguarding biological diversity is essential to the health of our planet, the resilience of our economies and the wellbeing of all people.”
One of the deal’s flagship goals was to protect at least 30 per cent of the world’s land, inland waters, coasts and oceans by 2030.
Yet even if current commitments are met, only 26 per cent of land and 12 per cent of the ocean would be protected by that deadline, the report finds.
Progress is also lagging on money, skills, cooperation and data, as well as on economic incentives that reward protecting nature rather than destroying it.
“This bad news means that the war on nature has not yet ended,” Mr. Guterres said at the report’s launch in Yerevan.
He warned that the world is still caught in three interlinked crises: climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution.
There has been some progress since 2022, however.
Nearly 90 per cent of countries that are parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity have set national targets, and more than half have drawn up their own plans to deliver them.
More than 70 per cent have measured and reported on their results.

Indigenous Peoples, local communities, regional and city authorities, charities and businesses have also made some 5,000 commitments – though the report warns of a serious gap between ambition and action.
Closing that gap will require money and expertise for developing countries on a far bigger scale, the report says.
Governments need to scrap subsidies that harm nature, strengthen social protection, redirect spending towards protecting nature and work with businesses on strong disclosure rules.
Better coordination is also needed between governments, business, civil society, young people, women and Indigenous Peoples to strengthen accountability, enforcement and cooperation.
“Biodiversity must be part of every decision being made – across policies, regulations and budgets,” Mr. Guterres said.
“Nature won’t thrive on good intentions.”
AI, green energy and economic transitions risk leaving vulnerable communities behind, UN warns

Rapid transformations – from artificial intelligence and digital technologies to renewable energy and demographic shifts – are reshaping economies worldwide, creating new opportunities but also threatening to deepen socio-economic inequalities, a new UN report warned on Thursday.
Benefiting from these changes often requires specialised skills and access to the latest technologies, putting disadvantaged groups at risk of being left behind.

Women, young people, older persons, persons with disabilities, migrants, Indigenous Peoples and low-income communities are particularly vulnerable, the report stresses, outlining recommendations for governments to ensure these transformations benefit everyone.
Social inclusion is a moral imperative, but it is also an economic necessity, the report from the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA) underlined.

It found that expanding opportunities to marginalised groups enlarges the productive workforce, strengthens human capital, increases innovation and entrepreneurship, improves labour allocation and spreads productivity gains more widely.
“Inclusive societies are more productive, resilient, and prosperous,” Secretary-General António Guterres summarised in a video message for the launch of the report.
Measures towards social inclusion should also be taken urgently, as those left outside key systems face steeper barriers to catching up later, the report emphasised.

As artificial intelligence transforms labour markets, the report urges governments to invest in continuous training and reskilling for workers whose jobs may be replaced or transformed, rather than focusing solely on creating new jobs.
Similarly, the shift to renewable energy must include support for workers and communities reliant on fossil fuels, through retraining, alternative employment opportunities and social assistance.
To bridge the digital divide, governments should also expand affordable access to the internet, digital infrastructure and technology training – particularly in disadvantaged communities.

One last major recommendation is to stop relying mainly on GDP to evaluate growth, and to also assess progress through poverty reduction, access to education and healthcare, employment security, inequality and environmental protection.
Economic growth that benefits only a small share of the population, it argues, cannot be considered genuinely inclusive.
Importantly, these investments require resources and many developing countries are facing financial constraints that could hamper the transition.

Nearly half of the world’s poorest countries are either in or at high risk of debt distress, with interest payments relative to revenue at their highest levels in a generation, the UN Secretary-General warned.
He called on leaders to live up to the commitments made through last year’s Doha Political Declaration on Social Development and the Sevilla Commitment on financing for development.
He also pushed for reform of international financial institutions to better represent and serve developing countries.
“Transformations are inevitable. Inequality and exclusion are not,” the UN Secretary-General said.
“Let’s work together to ensure that the profound transformations reshaping our world help build societies rooted in justice, dignity and opportunity for all.”

After a quiet start to the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, Isaias became the season’s first hurricane on October 8 as it tracked toward the U.S. Gulf Coast. The storm brought heavy rain and flash flooding to parts of the Southeast, including Alabama and the Florida Panhandle, and winds that toppled trees and downed power lines, leaving many people in the dark.

Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on the evening of October 9 as a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 miles (170 kilometers) per hour. Gusts topped 100 miles per hour along a corridor west of the storm’s center, according to the National Weather Service, with preliminary reports showing a 117-mile-per-hour gust in Oriole Beach and a 102-mile-per-hour gust at Pensacola City Hall.

These areas of high winds overlapped a broader area west of the storm’s eye where satellite images showed substantial decreases in nighttime lights. The image pair above shows nighttime lights before and after the storm. The left image is a composite of August 2026 data representing typical conditions, and the right image shows lights on October 11, after most of the storm’s clouds had cleared.

The data depicted in the images, provided by Ranjay Shrestha of NASA's Black Marble science team, come from the Black Marble HD product. The product uses data from the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-20 satellite, which has a day-night band that detects light emitted and reflected at night. The team processed the data to account for changes in the landscape, the atmosphere, and phase of the Moon, and to filter out stray light that does not come from electric lights. Dark gray, hash-marked areas show where clouds prevented VIIRS from collecting data. The nighttime lights are shown over a base map from the Landsat 9 satellite.

“Standard Black Marble nighttime lights imagery, available through NASA Worldview, provides a broad picture of the storm's immediate impacts,” Shrestha said. “Black Marble HD takes this a step further by allowing us to visualize these changes at a much finer spatial scale.”

At these finer scales, the images reveal lights decreasing sharply around parts of Pensacola, Florida, and along the U.S. Route 98 corridor toward Destin, suggesting widespread power disruptions. Shrestha also pointed out pockets where lights persisted, including Pensacola International Airport, Pensacola Christian College, and parts of downtown Pensacola. “These patterns could reflect backup power systems, differences in electrical infrastructure, or areas that maintained electricity during the storm, although the imagery alone cannot confirm the underlying reasons,” he said.

Black Marble HD images also reveal the pace and spatial patterns of recovery. The image pair above compares the same October 11 view (left) with one from October 12 (right), when lights had begun to return to some affected areas. By October 14, lighting patterns looked similar to pre-storm conditions.

“Understanding where recovery is progressing and where disruptions persist can help emergency responders and decision makers identify areas that may require additional attention, prioritize resources, and assess the effectiveness of restoration efforts,” Shrestha said.

Black Marble data complement ground-based outage reports rather than replace them, offering a more comprehensive view of disasters' impacts and recovery. “Ultimately, this is where the value of Black Marble lies: turning nighttime Earth observations into actionable insights that support informed decisions and help bridge the gap between Earth science and action,” Shrestha said.

The NASA Disasters Program, in coordination with FEMA and the USGS Coastal Storms Team, is supporting the Alabama Red Cross and the Alabama Emergency Management Agency’s response to Hurricane Isaias. The team will be posting maps and data products on its open-access mapping portal as new information becomes available.

A phenomenon rarer than a solar eclipse and more powerful than any single storm system is unfolding this fall, and NASA is tracking it closely.

El Niño is a natural climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific. NASA scientists are keeping watch as it flips trade winds, redistributes ocean heat, scrambles rain patterns, and raises sea surface height across parts of the Pacific.

As of October, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has said that there's an 83% chance that the strongest El Niño since 1950 is currently unfolding. People around the world, including farmers, firefighters, and coastal communities, are already experiencing the effects in different ways.
Follow along with these maps as NASA tracks El Niño from its epicenter in the equatorial Pacific Ocean.

One of the first clues appeared in satellite imagery in January 2026, when a swell of warm water called a Kelvin wave was spotted near Micronesia in the western Pacific. Kelvin waves are slow-moving pulses of water thousands of miles long. Like underwater freeways, they transfer heat from west to east across the Pacific. The warm water heats the air directly above it, making it rise. The change in air pressures weakens or even reverses the trade winds that typically blow in the opposing direction, from the Americas toward Asia, causing sea levels in the eastern Pacific to rise further, and waters to warm even more. This chain reaction signifies the start of an El Niño.

The map above shows that by early April, those Kelvin waves had reached the eastern Pacific, and sea surface temperatures had begun to warm. Warm water expands in volume, elevating local sea levels in some areas by as much as 1 to 1.3 feet (30 to 40 centimeters). The higher-than-normal water can be seen sloshing toward South America then moving up the coast to California. Sea levels that are six to eight inches (15 to 20 centimeters) lower than normal are visible around Indonesia and northern Australia.

“Kelvin waves are like the heartbeat of El Niño,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “And our sea level satellites let us peer into the ocean and watch every beat.”

Scientists have used satellite altimetry to track the height of the ocean with ultraprecision since 1993. That unbroken data record continues today with the Sentinel-6 satellites. State-of-the-art radar altimeters aboard these satellites survey millions of square miles of ocean in a single day, complementing NOAA’s fleet of ocean sensors and buoys drifting and diving through the water below.

Warmer-than-normal seawater is one of the best-known indicators of El Niño. Already, sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific are about 3 degrees Fahrenheit (1.7 degrees Celsius) warmer than the long-term average and could jump another fraction of a degree in the coming months, Willis said.

Satellites carrying microwave and infrared radiometers can see through and around clouds to measure heat energy at the sea surface. Satellites in 2026 mapped the band of warmer-than-normal water as it expanded throughout the spring. The band, seen in dark red, stretches for millions of square miles from the heart of the Pacific to the coast of South America. Ocean temperatures can influence weather patterns around the world. Air above the water’s surface carries heat and moisture into the atmosphere, seeding rainstorms and rearranging weather patterns across the globe.

El Niño’s warm waters also change the color of the ocean. A NASA satellite is tracking these subtle shifts in hues, as equatorial Pacific waters have become measurably more blue over the last several months.

“Some people think of water as being just blue, but it's amazing the multitude of colors the ocean can be,” said Matthew Kehrli, a lead research scientist for the PACE (Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem) satellite team at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.

This spectrum is in part thanks to microscopic plants called phytoplankton, which form the basis of the marine food web. There are thousands of different species of phytoplankton, which come in shades like teal, brown, or green. This year, in areas of the Pacific Ocean along the equator that are typically lush with phytoplankton and greener as a result, these hues are waning.

This is an expected effect of El Niño. Phytoplankton thrive in cool, nutrient-rich waters, but during an El Niño, the weakening trade winds reduce the upwelling of nutrient-rich deep water to the ocean surface. With limited food supply, phytoplankton abundance drops. This decline can trigger cascading effects across the marine food web, forcing other marine life to relocate to new feeding grounds.

This year’s El Niño is the first since PACE launched in 2024, providing new views of the phenomenon. The Ocean Color Instrument aboard PACE observes the ocean in hyperspectral color — across several hundred different wavelengths of visible, near-infrared, and ultraviolet light — monitoring phytoplankton and other ocean-color changes in near-real time. With PACE data, researchers calculate the average color of the ocean, simplifying spectra of light into a single number, known as apparent visible wavelength.

The 2026 map above shows the green area along the equator in the western Pacific Ocean shrink as a bluer shade fills in, indicating fewer phytoplankton. In contrast, the map from 2025 shows how the green-hued section stays steady over time.
“You have expectations of what you would think would happen,” Kehrli said. “But to visually see the results with the data products that you’re working with in real time is gratifying.”
NASA scientists will continue to monitor the signs and impacts of this El Niño with its fleet of Earth-observing satellites.
“El Niño touches almost all of us in some way every time it occurs,” Willis said. “While many have seen what it can do, we look to the ocean to understand why.”

How awesome would it be if the sun could take on a spooky green glow for Halloween? It turns out that scientists have discovered that our star may indeed go green, but only billions of years from now after its death — and only if it then starts eating planets like a cosmic zombie.

That's possible because scientists have discovered that white dwarfs, the type of stellar remnants sun-sized stars leave behind when they die, can actually take on a range of colors including green if they snack on their rocky planets like cosmic cannibals.

For stellar scientists, the colors of stars have always been indicative of their temperatures. Cool stars look orange, while stars like the sun look white, and the hottest stars glow pale blue. This is akin to a blacksmith's iron glowing red, then orange, then white-hot as it heats up. Researchers have always assumed that white dwarfs follow the same rule. However, new research suggests that these stellar corpses could glow in a range of colors including green, pink, cyan, yellow, and purple. That means the universe is far more colorful than we suspected.

"Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like 'perfect radiators,' so their color is set almost entirely by temperature. But nobody had really looked into what else might be possible for white dwarfs," team leader Mark Hollands of the University of Warwick said in a statement sent to Space.com.
"It turns out these incredibly dense stars caaaaan produce colors nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me."
How white dwarfs break stellar color rules

White dwarfs get their name because when they were discovered, they appeared surprisingly hot and glowed white or pale blue. However, this new research suggests that this slightly bland and uniform appearance is because no white dwarf is close enough for Earthbound astronomers to see their true colors.

The key to the rainbow-like array of colors this team suggests white dwarfs could possess is their density. White dwarfs form when stars with a mass roughly that of the sun run out of fuel and can no longer support themselves against their own gravity, causing their cores to collapse. As a result, the matter that makes up white dwarfs is around the density of water, millions of times denser than the sun's surface, the photosphere.

In these conditions, elements like carbon, calcium, and sodium can interact with the surrounding dense helium plasma and absorb light across a wider range of colors than they would at lower densities. That shifts the colors of white dwarfs away from the white/light blue seen for a perfect radiator of heat.
The researchers found that the colors of white dwarfs would fit into distinct groups tied to the individual chemical makeup of the stellar remnant's atmosphere.

White dwarfs abundant in carbon should be pink or purple, while those that have been enriched with debris from consumed asteroids and comets, and the remains of old planetary systems, would take a more yellow hue. Cooler white dwarfs with mixed hydrogen and helium atmospheres often would glow cyan or pale blue, caused as hydrogen molecules collide with helium atoms in their dense atmospheres.
One of the most striking examples of white dwarf coloration, however, would arise when one of these living dead stars starts feeding on the planets around it like a horror movie zombie.
The researchers found that some dead star white dwarfs can go a little green around the gills after snacking on orbiting planets.

An example of this is WD J1330+6435, a cool white dwarf located around 326 light-years away, which has been accreting rocky material from a planetary companion. This has enriched its atmosphere with calcium, lithium, and sodium, and the team's model suggests this would have led WD J1330+6435 to adopt a green hue.
But unlike the green-tinged zombies of George Romero's classic Dawn of the Dead, there are no hordes of these green-faced cosmic zombies ... yet.
The researchers think that no other star, living or dead, has ever been credibly reported as green. That makes WD J1330+6435 the first known genuinely green star.

"The traces of sodium in the atmosphere of this white dwarf absorb the orange part of the spectrum, leaving behind a ghostly green glow," Hollands said. "Imagine standing on a planet and looking up at a green star. It feels like something out of science fiction."
The team didn't just discover that a known white dwarf is the first-ever green star; they also discovered what could be the reddest star ever in the form of the white dwarf WD J1011+2845.

Located just 48 light-years from Earth, this white dwarf has a deep convection zone that carries carbon from its core to its surface. These carbon molecules distort light from the white dwarf, causing a deep salmon-pink glow unlike anything seen in any other star.

Despite this rainbow of white dwarfs, the team theorizes that white is still the most common color for these stellar corpses. Only five of the 151 white dwarfs within around 65 light-years of Earth have extraordinary coloring. Extrapolating this to the total population of white dwarfs, the team estimates that only one in 30 of these dead stars has an unusual color.

"One in thirty might not sound like a huge fraction, but across the entire population of white dwarfs in the universe, that is still a lot of oddly colored stars out there," Boris Gänsicke, Department of Physics, University of Warwick, said. "Yet if we take the median across a representative population of white dwarfs, we found that the average white dwarf really is white."
The team's research was published on Thursday (Oct. 14) in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments.

On Oct. 15, 1997, NASA launched the Cassini spacecraft on a mission to explore Saturn and its moons. It lifted off aboard a Titan 4B rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida.

It took almost seven years for the Cassini spacecraft to reach Saturn, with the spacecraft entering orbit around the ringed planet in 2004. Another smaller spacecraft called Huygens hitched a ride with Cassini, and it landed on Saturn's moon Titan in 2005.
Cassini spent 13 years studying the Saturn system up close, and the mission lasted about 20 years before coming to an epic grand finale on Sept. 15, 2017.
Running low on fuel, NASA chose to steer Cassini straight into Saturn's atmosphere, where the spacecraft was destroyed.

NASA's Cassini mission to Saturn (which carried the European Space Agency's Huygens lander to Titan) was a flagship planetary mission like no other ever when it first launched toward the ringed planet.

The $3.26 billion Cassini spacecraft became the first probe ever to orbit Saturn when it arrived in 2004. It revealed Saturn's rings as active and dynamic structures, as intricate and complex as they are beautiful to observe.
And it delivered Huygens to Titan, then followed up with a series of Titan flybys that revealed the cloudy moon could have liquid hydrocarbon rain, rivers, lakes and seas.
Perhaps the most exciting discoveries were the most surprising.

Cassini discovered a strange hexagon-shaped jetstream encircling Saturn's north pole and revealed massive hurricane-like vortexes over both of the planet's poles. In 2010, Cassini watched as a giant storm formed in Saturn's northern hemisphere, then grew to encircle the entire planet through 2011.

The spacecraft also discovered icy plumes of water erupting from Saturn's moon Enceladus, revealing new clues into that moon's subsurface ocean of liquid water, complete with hydrothermal events like those found in Earth's oceans.

It was to protect Enceladus, Titan and other Saturn moons that NASA ultimated sent Cassini into a death dive into Saturn at the end of its mission. The space agency wanted to prevent any chance of contamination at those pristine moons.

"NASA’s Cassini spacecraft and ESA’s Huygens probe expanded our understanding of the kinds of worlds where life might exist and eight more reasons the mission changed the course of planetary exploration," NASA said in an overview.

Scientists discover a surprising danger in smaller cancer cells

- Scientists have discovered that unusually small cancer cells carrying extra chromosomes can be far more aggressive than larger ones, growing faster, spreading more readily, and resisting common treatments. The surprising finding could help explain why some tumors are especially dangerous and provide a new way to predict cancer outcomes.
The discoveries emerged from years of painstaking laboratory work, including the careful examination of tumors grown in mice.

Graduate student Megan Sweet, who studies biological sciences at Virginia Tech, spends much of her time preparing extremely thin slices of tumor tissue. Working inside a refrigerated metal chamber, she carefully adjusts a mounted tumor, roughly the size of a pinkie fingernail, toward a sharp cutting blade.
"It's all about fine-tuning and making sure it's going to be an even slice," said Sweet, who studies biological sciences.
As the blade moves through the tissue, it produces a steady, rhythmic chopping sound.
"This is the hardest and most time-consuming part," Sweet said. "But it's also kind of meditative."

Each section is cut so thin that light can pass through it. Sweet carefully transfers the delicate tissue onto a glass slide, where selected cellular structures are stained to make them easier to distinguish under a powerful microscope.

The process involves repeated rounds of cutting, staining, examining, and comparing samples. Although painstaking, this work is helping scientists piece together why certain tumors become much more dangerous than others.

The Virginia Tech team has published findings that shed new light on how cancer develops and progresses. Their research was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, with additional findings published earlier this year in Cancer Research.
Most healthy cells in the human body are diploid, meaning they contain two complete sets of chromosomes, with one inherited from each parent.

Under normal conditions, these cells divide to produce new cells with the same chromosome arrangement. Occasionally, however, something goes wrong during division, leaving cells with an abnormal number of chromosomes.
When these errors are passed on during subsequent cell divisions, they can accumulate over time. Such changes are one of the ways cancer can develop.

For the past five years, Sweet and fellow graduate student Mat Bloomfield have worked with cell biologist Daniela Cimini to investigate cells carrying abnormal numbers of chromosomes, a common characteristic of cancer.
To study the consequences of these abnormalities, Cimini's team manipulated diploid cancer cells so they would duplicate their chromosomes without completing cell division.
The result was a type of cell known as a tetraploid cell, which contains four complete sets of chromosomes rather than the usual two.

These cells are not limited to laboratory experiments. Tetraploid cells can also emerge during the development of human tumors, and their presence has been associated with cancer progression and poorer outcomes for patients.
Cancer Cells Recruit Healthy Cells to Fuel Tumor Growth
Scientists have long recognized that tetraploid cells can make tumors more aggressive. What remained unclear was exactly how they contributed to cancer growth.
To investigate, Sweet and Bloomfield compared tumors that developed from ordinary diploid cancer cells with those formed from tetraploid cancer cells.
The experiments produced an unexpected result.
As tumors grew in mice, the proportion of tetraploid cells actually decreased. Despite this decline, the tumors continued expanding rapidly and reached substantial sizes.
The researchers discovered that tetraploid cancer cells were encouraging the recruitment of stromal cells, which are noncancerous connective tissue cells that help provide structural support.
These additional cells appeared to create an environment that favored further tumor development.
"The presence of even a small fraction of these tetraploid cells can promote the recruitment of extra non-cancerous cells that support further tumor progression," Sweet said.
The finding revealed a previously unrecognized mechanism through which abnormal cancer cells can promote tumor growth, even when they account for only a small portion of the tumor.
Smaller Cancer Cells Reveal a Surprising Danger
A separate investigation uncovered another unexpected connection between tetraploid cells and cancer aggressiveness.

Bloomfield was initially examining the physical characteristics of tetraploid cells. After producing tetraploid cells from human cancer cells and establishing colonies derived from individual cells, he noticed that the resulting groups were not all the same size.
Because tetraploid cells contain twice the usual number of chromosome sets, the researchers expected them to be approximately twice as large as diploid cells.
Instead, some of the cells were 25 to 30 percent smaller than anticipated.
Even more surprisingly, those smaller cells proved to be more capable of forming aggressive tumors than their larger counterparts.
"The smaller clones are more aggressive," Bloomfield said. "They grow faster, are more invasive, and more tolerant of common anti-cancer and stress-inducing drugs."
Further experiments in mice supported these observations. Tumors containing smaller tetraploid cells frequently grew more quickly than those containing larger ones.

The pattern was not restricted to a single type of cancer. Researchers observed similar results in both colorectal and breast cancer cells, suggesting that the relationship between tetraploid cell size and tumor aggressiveness may extend across different cancers.
Cancer Cell Size May Help Predict Patient Survival
The researchers next examined whether the same relationship could be found in human cancers.
They analyzed information from the Cancer Genome Atlas, a large collection of detailed data from thousands of cancer patient samples.
The results revealed that smaller tetraploid cells were associated with worse prognoses and lower survival rates across several cancer types.
This suggests that measuring the size of these abnormal cells could provide valuable information about how aggressively a tumor might behave.
"We already knew that tetraploidy can make cells more tumorigenic, but now we know that if you incorporate the size of the cells, it can be more predictive of tumorigenic potential," Cimini said.

The findings add an important dimension to scientists' understanding of cancer. Abnormal chromosome numbers have long been linked to dangerous tumor behavior, but the new research indicates that cell size may offer additional clues about a cancer's potential to grow and spread.
The team now plans to investigate the biological mechanisms responsible for these effects in greater detail while continuing to examine human cancer data.
For Sweet, that means more hours at the laboratory bench, carefully cutting and analyzing tiny sections of tumor tissue in the search for answers to one of cancer biology's most important questions.

Rare study reveals a striking divide inside an Alzheimerâs patientâs brain

- A rare examination of an Alzheimerâs patientâs brain revealed that regions cleared of amyloid plaques had remarkably little of the harmful tau buildup associated with memory loss, while neighboring areas showed extensive damage. The discovery suggests that removing amyloid may have lasting protective effects and could help slow Alzheimerâs progression, especially when treatment begins early.

An unusually detailed examination of an Alzheimer's patient's brain has revealed striking differences between regions where treatment successfully removed harmful amyloid plaques and areas where those plaques remained. The regions cleared of amyloid showed little or no buildup of tau tangles, another protein abnormality strongly associated with brain cell damage and declining memory. Nearby areas that still contained amyloid, however, showed much higher levels of tau and evidence of continued neurodegeneration.

The discovery offers rare evidence from a human brain that removing amyloid plaques may provide protection against other damaging processes involved in Alzheimer's disease (AD). The results also suggest that clearing amyloid thoroughly, particularly early in the disease, could help limit tau accumulation and slow the progression of brain damage.

Researchers from the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania presented the findings at the 2026 Alzheimer's Association International Conference. The study was also published in JAMA.

"Seeing both disease patterns side-by-side in the same brain gave us a rare opportunity to understand how amyloid removal affects other proteins that contribute to Alzheimer's disease," said co-senior author David Wolk, MD, co-director of the Penn Memory Center and director of the Penn Alzheimer's Disease Research Center. "The findings provide some of the clearest human evidence to date that anti-amyloid therapies may limit the accumulation of tau and slow the brain changes that lead to memory loss and cognitive decline."
How Amyloid and Tau Contribute to Alzheimer's Disease

Two proteins play major roles in the development of Alzheimer's disease. Beta-amyloid collects outside nerve cells, forming sticky deposits known as plaques. Tau, meanwhile, accumulates inside neurons and forms abnormal tangles. Both are associated with the progressive damage to brain cells that contributes to memory problems, changes in personality, and difficulties with thinking.

Treatments designed to eliminate amyloid plaques have significantly changed how Alzheimer's is managed in recent years. Aducanumab became the first drug of this type to receive accelerated approval from the FDA, although it is no longer sold. Since then, newer and more effective medications that target amyloid through a similar approach, donanemab (Kisunla) and lecanemab (Leqembi), have received full FDA approval.

Researchers have long believed that amyloid buildup helps create the conditions in which harmful tau tangles develop. What has been much harder to establish is whether eliminating amyloid can also limit tau accumulation in the human brain.
Direct evidence has been scarce because relatively few people who received amyloid-clearing drugs have undergone brain examinations after death.
A Rare Brain Examination Reveals a Striking Pattern
The researchers were able to investigate this question using brain tissue donated by a former Alzheimer's clinical trial participant.

The man was in his fifties when he was diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment caused by Alzheimer's disease. He subsequently joined a clinical trial testing aducanumab and received 30 doses of the medication over four and a half years.

He died approximately four years after his last dose, more than a decade after his first symptoms appeared. Before his death, he expressed a wish to donate his brain to scientific research. The tissue was provided to the Center for Neurodegenerative Disease Research in the Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine.
When specialists examined the donated brain, they discovered an unusual pattern in which neighboring regions showed dramatically different amounts of Alzheimer's-related damage.

The raised ridges of the brain's folded surface, known as gyri, had lost most of their amyloid plaques and contained very little accumulated tau. In contrast, the neighboring grooves between these ridges, called sulci, still contained considerable amyloid buildup. These regions also exhibited substantially more tau tangles, inflammation, and degeneration of brain tissue.
This patchwork distribution was consistent with scans taken while the patient was alive, which had already indicated that amyloid removal varied considerably across different parts of his brain.

"Many previous reports have shown either extensive amyloid clearance or limited clearance," said co-senior author Edward B. Lee, MD, PhD, the John Q. Trojanowski, MD, PhD Professor for Neurodegenerative Disease Research in Pathology and Laboratory Medicine. "This case represented a unique 'Goldilocks' scenario in which some regions cleared amyloid and others did not. It allowed us to directly compare what happened next in neighboring brain regions and better understand the relationship between amyloid, tau, and neurodegeneration."
Could Alzheimer's Treatments Protect the Brain for Years?
The findings could have important implications for the latest generation of Alzheimer's medications, which remove amyloid using mechanisms similar to the therapy received by this patient.

Although the investigation involved only one individual, the contrast between different brain regions suggests that substantial amyloid removal may influence other disease processes long after treatment has stopped.

The results also raise an important question about how the benefits of Alzheimer's drugs are measured. Clinical trials commonly evaluate patients over approximately 18 months, but some protective effects might take considerably longer to become apparent.

However, the study cannot establish how much amyloid must be removed to achieve lasting protection or prove that plaque clearance was directly responsible for the differences in tau accumulation and brain damage.

Researchers now hope to understand why certain parts of the brain respond more effectively to amyloid-clearing treatments than others. Identifying and potentially strengthening the biological mechanisms responsible for plaque removal could lead to better therapies.
Another major question is whether beginning treatment before extensive tau tangles develop could substantially delay Alzheimer's or even prevent the disease from emerging.
Why Earlier Alzheimer's Treatment Could Matter

Because amyloid can accumulate silently in the brain for many years before memory problems begin, researchers are increasingly interested in treating people during the earliest stages of the disease, potentially before noticeable symptoms appear.

"Patients may accumulate amyloid for years before symptoms appear," said first author Christopher A. Brown, MD, PhD, an assistant professor of Neurology. "This case suggests that removing amyloid early may help limit the changes that ultimately damage brain cells. Ongoing trials will help determine whether starting treatment before symptoms begin can provide even greater benefit."

If there is extraterrestrial life out there, it's certainly done a great job of staying hidden so far (at least as far as the official scientific consensus goes).

International researchers led by a team from the University of Osaka in Japan have now developed a new electrical technique for spotting signs of life outside of Earth's atmosphere – and it promises to be simpler than current approaches to alien detection.
The method focuses on amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, and details have been published in Nature Communications.
Amino acids come in two mirror-image forms, the L-form and the D-form, and the balance between them in a sample can indicate if the amino acids were produced by something living or non-living.

In scientific terms, the form (or 'handedness') of an amino acid is called its chirality, and the technique developed by the researchers can spot this chirality using a tiny gap between two gold nanowires.
"The single-molecule detection and discrimination of molecular chirality demonstrated here highlight a fundamental advance in chemical sensing," write the researchers in their published paper.

Amino acid chirality can already be analyzed using an approach called liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS), but the instruments needed for it are bulky and require large samples and multiple chemical processes. It's not ideal for packing onto the back of a lunar buggy.
What the researchers have developed here is much, much smaller.
The two gold nanowires are barely separated from each other and create an electrical tunneling current between them – a quantum effect where electrons 'leak' across the gap.

As a solution containing amino acid molecules is dropped onto a microchip holding the gap, the current changes in a way that can be measured, revealing which forms the amino acids are in. Machine learning was used to identify the L-form and D-form molecules from the electrical spikes.

"By combining our nanogap tunneling technique with artificial intelligence, we were able to distinguish between the L and D-forms of amino acids with over 80 percent accuracy," says bioengineer Takahito Ohshiro, from the University of Osaka.
"This is the first discrimination of amino-acid chirality at the single-molecule level."

It's going to take more testing and development to get this into a fully working amino acid scanner that can be added to an astronaut's toolkit, but the researchers have already tested the approach against current methods.
"We analyzed natural samples from the Murchison meteorite in Australia and soil samples from the Atacama Desert in Chile," says nanotechnologist Masateru Taniguchi, from the University of Osaka.
"Our method was comparable to traditional methods, as both were capable of capturing the major features of amino acid composition."

Of course, this isn't a long-range alien life detector – we're still going to have to get hold of samples to test – but the nanogap device promises a relatively straightforward, compact testing mechanism that needs less preparation and requires fewer molecules.

Potentially, it could be fitted on probes and rovers without a human crew, perhaps beaming back news about signs of life discovered on distant moons and planets. That's still some way off for now, though.

One of the challenges researchers need to overcome next is preparing the sensor for molecules that it may not have come across before or been trained on. The machine learning component here was crucial to the study's success.

The technology is now ready to be taken further – for chemical analysis on Earth as well as beyond – and if we do one day detect life on an alien landscape, this might be the approach that makes the discovery.

"These results establish a targeted single-molecule electrical approach for chiral amino acid analysis and provide a foundation for future applications to study chemically complex samples, including those relevant to astrobiological research," write the researchers.
The research has been published in Nature Communications.

Published in Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology, the comprehensive study analyzes data from 199,155 individuals, with a median age of 59. Participants are enrolled in ongoing health research and complete food and lifestyle questionnaires every 2–4 years.

The authors of the new study, from Oregon Health and Science University (OHSU) and Massachusetts General Hospital, found a 28 percent higher risk of cirrhosis and a 36 percent higher risk of MASLD among late-night eaters compared to those with more standard eating times.
Late-night eating was defined as eating "after bedtime" or "between dinner and bedtime."
To put that increased risk into perspective, cirrhosis remained uncommon, with 315 cases among nearly 200,000 participants over the follow-up period.
The researchers think that our circadian rhythms, the built-in cycles that sync our bodies with daytime and nighttime, may explain the link.
"A few studies have hinted at this idea, but this is among the first long-term analyses to explicitly draw the connection to fatty liver disease," says hepatologist Robert Wilechansky, from OHSU.

"We know the liver is very much in tune with the body's circadian rhythms. So we're interested in changing the timing of eating in a way that could make a difference in health, without changing the composition of what people eat."

The median follow-up time for the study was 16 years, with adjustments made to factor in variables including age, body mass index (BMI), and physical activity. The late-night eating association remained significant after the adjustments.

While the study can't prove direct cause and effect, and other factors might be at play here – sleep timing and quality weren't accounted for in this analysis, for example – the researchers suggest that the different way the body processes food at night could be having an influence.
We all have multiple circadian clocks running in our bodies, and the liver does its own timekeeping as well as connecting to the main circadian rhythms.

It's possible that the liver isn't prepared to efficiently deal with food late into the evening, resulting in more fat building up and blood sugar levels rising – though these ideas will need further testing.
"Our findings add to the growing body of literature linking late-evening eating patterns to adverse metabolic and liver outcomes," write the researchers in their published paper.
"This relationship is biologically plausible; higher evening caloric intake may lead to obesity and metabolic derangement via decreased insulin sensitivity and lower energy utilization at night."

Further research could look at exactly what late-night eating consisted of – in this analysis the snacking time was logged, but not the snack – as well as measuring indicators like blood sugar and liver fat more directly.
An OHSU team that includes Wilechansky is already recruiting for a more thorough clinical trial.
"The effects of late-evening food intake on liver disease should be further studied in diverse populations, incorporating liver imaging and markers of liver disease severity," write the researchers.
"Confirmation of these results would have the potential to impact best practices in nutrition for chronic liver disease."

MASLD, also known as fatty liver disease, is when metabolic issues (such as obesity) lead to fat building up in the liver. In some people, it can cause scarring, which can then lead to cirrhosis, where the liver is permanently damaged and can eventually start to fail.

Knowing more about how these two conditions are triggered or exacerbated will help with prevention and treatments going forward. It could be that one way of reducing your risk of liver disease is as simple as being disciplined about eating times – an easier ask than a diet or exercise regime.
"We are seeing over and over again that the timing of behaviors, whether it's sleep, eating or exercise, really matters," says sleep and circadian physiologist Andrew McHill, from OHSU.
The research has been published in Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology.

Quantum computers promise exponential computational power by processing many possibilities simultaneously. But the machines we have today are still far from this ideal. For one, their bits, called qubits, are prone to frequent errors, and as a result, quantum computers are limited for now. To overcome errors, the machines need to tap into so-called magic states—and scientists at Google Research think their quantum chip could help get them there. In a new study published today in Science, the researchers show how to supply magic states more cheaply using a gardening-inspired technique called cultivation.

Traditional computers build every calculation from a few simple logic gates, such as AND, OR and NOT. By contrast, “quantum computers have their own analogy of these operations called the Clifford gates,” explains Emma Rosenfeld, a researcher at Google Quantum AI and the study’s lead author. Clifford gates, however, can be imitated by a normal computer. “But there is one particular gate that unlocks the quantum computer’s power,” Rosenfeld says. “Physicists call it a non-Clifford gate, most often a T gate.” This extra gate is produced using a magic state.

A quibit in a magic state is prepared in a very specific blend of the states 0 and 1 (occupying a mixture of states is a specialty of quantum computers). Fed into a calculation, it is used up to perform the extra gate, and any flaw in the state becomes a flaw in the gate. “It has to be made very, very precisely,” Rosenfeld says.

The standard recipe to make magic states is called distillation, and it creates fewer, more accurate quantum states from many imperfect ones. “You can have up to 95 percent of your quantum computer being spent just generating these high-fidelity magic states,” Rosenfeld says. To bypass this bottleneck, in 2024 her colleagues at Google Research proposed an alternative technique called cultivation, which works on a single state.

Using Google’s Willow chip, Rosenfeld’s team encoded a rough magic state in a few qubits and then measured it. Measuring a quantum state typically collapses it, forcing it into one of two possible answers. So instead of asking the question, “Are you 0 or 1?” which collapses the quantum state to either of those two options, the team asked, “Are you the right magic state: yes or no?”

States that pass this test are then spread across more qubits for stronger protection, hence the gardening name: the state starts small, gets checked and then grows. Without cultivation, about four attempts in 1,000 produced a faulty state. With it, errors fell by roughly 40-fold. The experiment used 54 physical qubits out of Willow’s 105.

“The Google experiment shows that cultivation works in practice,” says Kenneth Brown, director of the Duke Quantum Center at Duke University, who was not involved in the study. He notes, however, that the technique relies on a quality assurance step that rejects low-quality states, discarding 92 percent of attempts.

The result is still far from what practical applications demand. For example, using a quantum computer to break the current RSA-2048 encryption employed in website security, banking and electronic ID cards would require magic states that would fail only once in 10 billion tries. To simulate molecules, a use Rosenfeld says is more attainable, we would need such states with only one error in a million to one in 100 million. Right now the team stands at roughly one error in 10,000 attempts. Still, the new work represents a step in the right direction, she says.
“We’re more galvanized than ever to get to these near-term scientific applications,” Rosenfeld says.
What if we could turn the Red Planet green?

The idea of Mars made verdant with grasses, trees and other Earthly life-forms may sound like science fiction, but at least one small group of scientists and engineers is working to make it a reality. Pioneer Labs, a nonprofit research organization led by CEO Erika DeBenedictis, recently announced what it calls “the first microbe for Mars”: a microorganism adapted to Martian conditions that might someday help humans survive there, too.

Such bioengineered bugs could, in principle, allow astronauts to better “live off the land” on Mars by converting the planet’s raw resources into building materials for habitats, fertilizers for crops, and other products. But the broader vision of Pioneer Labs is far more audacious and fraught: to use biology to help transform Mars into a more habitable and Earth-like world. Terraforming remains a distant and deeply speculative prospect beset by enormous scientific and engineering challenges. It also raises fundamental questions about whether and how humans should ever deliberately unleash Earth life on an alien world.

Scientific American sat down with DeBenedictis to explore the scientific promise, technical hurdles and ethical dilemmas of sending bioengineered terrestrial microorganisms to Mars. What could such organisms realistically accomplish? How close are we to deploying them beyond Earth? And what obligations do we have to preserve a world where the past or present existence of indigenous life remains uncertain? The answers to these questions could ultimately help shape a larger debate about humanity’s extraterrestrial future—and whether the impulse to make other worlds more like our own should be tempered by any obligation to leave them undisturbed.
