It’s the very first step toward this bigger picture—this really inspiring vision of terraforming Mars and making it a habitable, beautiful place.
So this microbe—what’s so special about it, and what exactly is it supposed to do?

What’s cool about it is that we’ve engineered it so that it can directly use the nutrients in Martian regolith, water and processed atmosphere—which is really useful! The idea is that you can go to Mars, and you can feed it dirt, water and air, and use it to build bioplastic houses for astronauts.

Yeah. This is a derivative of a terrestrial bacterium called Cupriavidus necator, which naturally produces bioplastic kind of for the same reason that when you eat too many doughnuts, you put on weight in your hips. When this organism has too much carbon around, it creates these big vacuoles of bioplastics, which is a class of materials we’re all familiar with in everyday life. We use them to make everything from compostable cups to 3D printing filament—and that’s essentially how we’d like to make houses on Mars.

So the astronaut houses would have these 3D-printed panels that hold up the structure, and then it would have this plastic lining that holds in the pressure so that you can breathe and that also shields you from radiation.
We’re calling this engineered microbe sPL.001—a special strain made by Pioneer Labs, and the very first of several, in fact. We’ve got plans for four more.

Something to help you build houses seems like a pretty good first step. You mentioned there are more microbes in the works. Presumably they’d do other things—because if we’re trying to build some kind of self-sustaining habitat on Mars, we need obviously more than just big domes made of bioplastic, right?

Absolutely. So let me give you some context first: we’re called Pioneer Labs, and that name is referring to this ecological idea of a pioneer species. On Earth, nature is really good at taking hostile environments—like after a volcanic eruption or a forest fire—and rebuilding a complex ecosystem one step at a time, and the very first steps are executed by really hardy organisms called pioneer species.

They’re often lichens. My favorite, though, is dandelions. They can grow in these really harsh environments, and their presence makes that environment more hospitable for a wider diversity of organisms.

I need to be clear, though: this very first microbe, sPL.001, can’t grow outside on its own on Mars, and that’s important because we don’t want to contaminate Mars accidentally. Yet it’s useful for making these habitats that more stuff can grow in. We think there are four other microorganisms that could complement this first one; altogether we think this could scale up to let us make arable land that’s suitable for agriculture—growing beautiful green plants and making food.
So we’ve talked about this first one for helping to build shelters on Mars. What about the others?

We have candidates for the others now, so nothing is finalized yet, but the idea is each additional microbe type can be another step in this ecological succession for Mars. So consider this a sneak peek.

About half the team is now working on windows. Because if you want to make greenhouses, for instance, you need transparent materials to let the sunlight in. And ideally you’d be able to manufacture those at scale with biology. Imagine growing microbes in a pond that secrete something that floats to the surface, and then you can peel what will become a nice big greenhouse panel right off the top.

And the other half of our team is working on getting rid of the perchlorate in Martian regolith. Perchlorate is a compound that’s poisonous to humans, and there’s so much of it there that Mars dirt can be poisonous to humans, too, as it is now. But there are microbes we’ve found that are able to eat that toxin and degrade it. We’ve found some actually that can eat it directly out of simulated Mars dirt—just add water! So now we just have to push the concentrations up, because Mars has more perchlorate than any organism on Earth has ever experienced naturally. And just like with all our other work, we’re using evolution to try to make an organism that can tolerate it.

Okay. And so the whole idea is that by growing these things locally—by living off the land, so to speak—you’re able to be more efficient and cost-effective, and ultimately self-sustaining, because you don’t have to bring everything from Earth?

Yeah. The reason we haven’t already done a human mission is that humans, with all our radiation shielding and food and so on, are just so heavy. And it’s just so hard to get that much mass to Mars to allow people live for a period of time, and then it’s even harder to bring them back. So it’s incredibly helpful to use resources that are on-site. And indeed, that’s what frontier civilizations have always done.

I want to be upfront about my own biases here: I think this is such a cool idea. But as with pretty much every other aspirational project related to human spaceflight, let alone otherworldly settlement, this one has its critics, too. And I think if I could summarize the sorts of criticisms I’ve seen, it would be three interlinked questions: Why terraforming? Why Mars? And why now?
That is, assuming these bioengineered bugs could also be really useful on Earth, why not just focus your efforts here?

You and I and everyone who’s ever lived is really lucky to live on the one planet we know of that has a functional biosphere. That’s why we’re here breathing, right, because we have a whole planet worth of photosynthesis that’s cranking out oxygen for us all the time. We just call it “nature” and tend to take it for granted.

When we go to space, nature is the one thing that we’re missing. It’s the thing we leave behind when we go away from Earth. Well, I love the biosphere, and I think we should bring it with us. I would love for any future humanity that ventures off into the stars to have more interaction with all sorts of delightful types of life rather than less.

This runs counter to typical visions for the future, I think, where there’s this tendency to think that progress means less nature and fewer trees and we all live in cities with big skyscrapers. That makes me sad, and I don’t think it has to be that way, and so I’m trying to fix it.

Mars specifically is this fascinating world in part because it’s almost like a long-lost twin of Earth. Four billion years ago, both planets had liquid water. And Mars, to this day, even after its climate has been substantially altered, still has all the raw materials for life in abundance in a way that the moon doesn’t and that even Venus doesn’t. Venus doesn’t have a lot of water left, and Mars does—it’s got a whole northern hemisphere that’s permafrost, with huge amounts of buried ice. If only we could warm it up, Mars might become a pretty nice place to live.

And I think that the instinct to go searching outward is just a thing people have. Not everyone wants to be an explorer, but for people who do, Mars is this incredibly intriguing target. And whoever goes first, I’d love for them to have flowers when they live somewhere that’s not Earth.
Flowers on Mars! Maybe it’ll be a dandelion, even.
That would be Pioneer species number six, ha.

Your announcement of sPL.001 made quite a splash, of course. I’m wondering, though, outside of the millions of people who saw your social media post or watched the slick promotional video introducing Pioneer Labs, what the reactions have been from some of your peers in bioengineering, planetary science, astrobiology, and so on. Has it been mixed?

So far, the reaction has been overwhelmingly positive. And I think that’s partially because we took our time preparing for this. We didn’t just announce that we’d engineered the first organism for Mars. We also released a paper showing how we did it, a second paper about a proposed planetary protection framework for thinking about the risks of actually sending such things to Mars and a third paper offering a complete techno-economic analysis for the use cases.

We’ve shown sPL.001 would be extremely dead if it gets outside on Mars, so, in many ways, this is less risky than sending a human complete with a diverse and complex microbiome on her skin and in her gut. And we’ve shown how this could actually be useful, right—not just how to grow the organism but all of the equipment that has to surround it in order to feed it, heat it, purify products from it and actually build houses. We’ve quantified how much all that mass is, how many launches you’d need to get it to Mars and the total footprint it would have.

So we really put our best work into trying to introduce this idea to people in a way that shows why it’s so cool and valuable but also is thoughtful about the ethics. This work has value even if we never terraform Mars. Practically speaking, this is just a good thing to do for the first human mission.

And so—especially on X, where this really went viral—I think there were more people who applauded the fact that we had also released a paper about the ethics than there were people who were like, “Er, we should never go to Mars.”
You’d have to go over on Bluesky to see more of those reactions, I think.

Let me try to “both sides” this a bit. I want to double down on the very valid point you’re making: if we’re trying to weigh risk and potential impact, landing a single human—or even a single piece of human excrement, let’s say—on Mars, that’s an orders-of-magnitude bigger deal than landing an enclosed bioreactor.

But I also inquired about the reactions of your peers because peer review is important in science, and it’s not clearly something that’s happened for any of those three papers you mentioned. There’s a disclaimer near the end of each one that basically says this has not and will not be submitted for peer-reviewed publication because that goes against the “open science” policy of the Astera Institute, a billionaire-backed nonprofit for incubating transformative science and technology that partly funded the work.

So with that in mind, I have to ask: Who is independently evaluating this stuff? You’re saying that it’s safe to send sPL.001 to Mars, and in the second paper that you mentioned, yes, you’re proposing a protocol for ensuring that nothing bad can happen in terms of biocontamination. But who’s validating these assertions? That seems like a pretty important step in the process, so I’m wondering why you’re skipping it.

My hope is for us to get to share the science we’re doing openly and very quickly. And I should say that we at Pioneer Labs don’t make NASA policy—and that NASA, in fact, isn’t the only organization that makes policy for the whole world, either. There are a lot of discussions that have already been happening about how to update things like planetary protection frameworks for the upcoming new era of human interplanetary spaceflight.

We clearly need new frameworks. Historically, NASA policy has been to stringently sterilize everything that goes to Mars, and you obviously can’t do that for a living human! So we’ve decided to throw our hat in the ring and make suggestions about what that new framework could look like. The goal of the Planetary Protection paper we released is for it to be discussed by COSPAR [the Committee on Space Research], which is the main body that makes policy suggestions to the world. My co-founder Una Nattermann will also be on NASA’s newly convened M-FORCE tiger team, which will make recommendations to COSPAR. Our goal here is to participate in the discussion.

And similarly, we’ve made suggestions about what it could look like to do the first biomanufacturing on Mars. We call this a “reference architecture,” which is a type of paper or engineering document that the space science community often uses. These aren’t usually published in a traditional science journal. I think space science is a discipline that certainly sometimes uses peer review to great effect, but not all of the science happens specifically through journals.

We do currently have funding from the Astera Institute, which believes very strongly that the current peer review journal system is incredibly toxic for science and for innovation. I don’t think anyone really disagrees with that. But as you say, there is this downside to being forced not to participate in traditional journals, which is getting this question about who certifies it. We have, ahead of time, already shared these papers with various colleagues, some of whom are acknowledged in them for the feedback they provided.

Also, there’s no stamp of approval, including from a journal, that means something is definitely right, which means even if we did send it to a journal, that doesn’t mean it’s better. We’re just trying to do the best science we can, and part of the challenge is we have to chart new territory about what it looks like to do this without this kind of crutch of journals dictating what is correct—which we all know to not be true anyway.

I should say the question doesn’t necessarily come from an adversarial place. You’ve stated elsewhere that Pioneer Labs is hopeful to hit the 2031 launch window for Mars. And that’s practically tomorrow, as far as developing a payload and securing a rocket ride is concerned, right? So it would seem in your best interest to try to bring everybody on board, so to speak, as quickly and fully as possible by addressing any significant concerns that exist.
Relatedly, maybe, I wonder if there’s anything you could tell me about what that 2031 mission would notionally look like?

Yeah, I agree. Flight testing is incredibly difficult in terms of the amount of prep that needs to go into it and the magnitude of engineering that needs to go right. That’s even more true for a Mars mission because Mars is so far away. So we’ve released that third paper, the reference architecture, in part because we’re interested to see how the space science community reacts, especially to different possibilities for what the first flight test could look like.

Here’s one example of what the first flight test could be. Wouldn’t it be so cool to go to Mars and do a search-for-life experiment there, where you take a scoop of Mars dirt, you add water, and you incubate it and see if anything grows? Because Mars had nice liquid water back when there was very nascent life on Earth, and there seem to have been giant impacts ping-ponging around the solar system—so maybe one of those impacts sent something to Mars, and maybe today it’s not growing because Mars is too harsh. Maybe it’s dormant in the soil or the ice. One way to find it would be an “enrichment”-type search-for-life experiment. You could sample some dirt or ice, see if it grows anything under more hospitable conditions and do the same after adding fertilizers to see if it’s nutrient-limited.

Now in order to do that experiment correctly, you do need a positive control, so you need to know that your device worked and that stuff can grow in it, and here is where the first microbe we engineered comes in. You could bring sPL.001 as your positive control and confirm that, yes, this organism that’s been carefully selected to die if it gets outside on Mars can in fact grow in a sealed container using the nutrients in Mars dirt.

I think this would be great for everyone. Like, the best-case scenario is you find life on Mars—but even if you don’t, by testing this organism’s growth on Mars you’ve now derisked this big thing that would allow you in the next test to actually use it for engineering and biomanufacturing.

So this is one possible example of a pretty small first step toward deliberately sending terrestrial life to Mars. It’s safer than sending a human. It has some basic science benefit. And it can be scaled up to do things like testing a larger bioreactor—depending on how big a step the space science community feels comfortable taking and which scientific risks we want to address and eliminate.

Speaking of scientific risks, the loudest critics I’ve seen of this work are astrobiologists interested in finding life on Mars who worry that something like sPL.001, if sent there, still poses unacceptable chances for contaminating the planet and irreparably sabotaging the search. Then there’s the more extreme ethical criticism of possible terraforming, perhaps best summarized by the late, great Carl Sagan: “If there is life on Mars..., Mars then belongs to the Martians, even if the Martians are only microbes.”
Yeah, I don’t agree with that second one.

In general, human astronauts on Mars would massively expand our ability and flexibility to search for life. The search for life doesn’t end because you’ve sent humans. Here on Earth, we still go out and look for dinosaur bones even though we already know they’re there. On Mars, the search could and would continue, which reflects something good about humans. We’re curious about our surroundings and we want to know more, and I think that’s something we should encourage.

It’s really complicated, of course, but here are some simple facts to think about. Here on Earth, we have a word for being vegetarian. But we don’t even have a word for trying not to eat microbes, because it’s totally infeasible! There are many different types of life deserving of our respect, but that doesn’t mean a very simple life-form on Mars should unduly eliminate any possible benefit humans could gain by going there.

I think we’re overdue for a big-picture shift in our approach to Mars, which we’ve been treating solely as this object of scientific study, with incredibly strict protocols for what you can send there and how sterile it needs to be—because this isn’t the only relationship that we could have with Mars, right? Like, humanity could live on Mars, and in that scenario, you then have to weigh the potential value of the scientific knowledge of the planet’s history and its former or extant life against the value of humanity having another home.

And just practically speaking, I do think humans are gonna go to Mars someday, so we have to figure out how to do it in a thoughtful way that sets us up for success in living there, as well as in understanding the planet and its history. I don’t think the answer is to get totally tied in knots and paralyzed by the ethics.

That brings me to my final question. You’ve stated in various places that you hope within your lifetime to look up at the little red dot of Mars in Earth’s sky and see that it’s slightly tinged with green—presumably from imported terrestrial life. What do you think is the biggest hurdle to overcome for that? Would it be scientific, technical, political, ethical?

If you had asked me this question two years ago when we began, I would say the biggest hurdle is a technical one. That’s why I was excited to work on sPL.001—because I perceived myself as someone who knows how to solve science problems, and I was looking for a big juicy target to sink my teeth into.

And now when you ask me, I actually do think maybe the hurdle is more social and political in a similar way to how on Earth we struggle to figure out the collective action puzzle of who pays for addressing climate change. Part of why I like working on the Mars case is that I think in some ways it’s much simpler. There’s no NIMBYism on Mars. And I’m hopeful that together, both the technical and the social things that need doing to make humans on Mars happen could be useful right here on Earth, too.

Everything is a computer these days. Fridges, washing machines, televisions, and more are now outfitted with computer chips to give them new capabilities, and manufacturers called them “smart” even before ChatGPT came out. Now, though, researchers have strung 15 cheap TV boxes together to run an artificial intelligence model, raising the possibility that the computers inside these everyday gadgets could someday help spread autonomous, AI-powered malware.

On Monday Anthropic released a blog post exploring this sort of attack. Researchers at the company tested how AI models might act as computer worms, programs that move between devices and leave copies of themselves behind, among everyday household gadgets. A worm that runs on smart devices instead of relying on a data center could prove difficult to shut down. Anthropic’s experiments suggest how that might happen—though they stop short of demonstrating the full threat.

Typically, large language models (LLMs) are trained and run in data centers, which can contain hundreds of thousands of specialized chips called graphics processing units, or GPUs. “Just because you don’t have a big GPU doesn’t mean that you can’t be a host to one of these models,” says Jeffrey Ladish, founder and executive director of Palisade Research, a California-based AI safety nonprofit that studies the risk of AI systems slipping beyond human control, past malware to rogue behavior.

In recent months, researchers have experimented with various types of computer worms, stapling AI models onto them to make them adaptive and harder to kill. Here, though, the researchers explored whether an AI model itself could be distributed as the worm, spreading its weights to new devices and running across even weak chips.
"Anybody with an open-weight model, with the right prompts and by brute-force luck, can find these worms," says computer scientist Vyas Sekar.

Specifically, researchers working on Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team showed two key capabilities. First, they were able to split up a relatively small model—one from Google DeepMind’s open-weight Gemma line—across 15 TV boxes they had bought and networked themselves so that they could run the entire model by chaining these boxes together. Each individual box was too weak to run the model on its own. But LLMs can be split into layers, an arrangement in which each layer manipulates the data it receives and passes that revised data to the next layer. By giving each box the job of handling just a couple of these layers, the team was able to run Gemma entirely and get responses back from just the weak chips in these boxes.

After that, the researchers tested how an AI worm might spread across devices in a virtual sandbox. A larger model—from the Chinese start-up Z.ai—managed to get a smaller model—one of Meta’s Llama models—running on the targets. But the larger model was too large to run on those weak devices itself, and it still relied on a separate server. This means the team did not show an AI worm capable of spreading and running itself on such devices. Anthropic argues that as small models become more capable, one could eventually use both methods.

The research also raises the prospect of adaptation and improvement by suggesting that AI models could subsist on low-power devices and drift through the Internet, getting better at spreading as they go. Anthropic makes this clear in its blog post about the work, concluding that AI systems could soon be “passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves.”

Ladish believes the main lesson from the research is in how AI models could divvy up work across computers of all shapes and sizes. “Basically, compute is a resource that these models can use,” he says, pointing to everything from Apple MacBooks to data centers to everyday objects like smart TVs as possible sources of computing power if attackers can hack them.

Not everyone thinks that the experiments amount to a new kind of threat, however. “I think there’s some caution that’s needed here to make sure we talk about what capabilities are new and transformative,” says Michael Bailey, a professor studying computer systems security at the Georgia Institute of Technology. He emphasizes avoiding “fearmongering” with the lessons taken away from this kind of work. Researchers already know how insecure devices like TV boxes can be. “We already had self-replicating malware,” says Bailey. “We had botnets.”

“All of these are classical computer security threats,” adds Vyas Sekar, a professor of computer engineering at Carnegie Mellon University. According to Sekar, the bigger problem is that more people might be able to launch such attacks—a “democratization of being evil,” as he calls it. Sekar thinks this makes monitoring and restricting data flow between smart devices even more important.

Even the risk of hijacking raw computing power on chips is not new. Hackers have long taken over other people’s computers to mine cryptocurrency. So while smart devices could face new attacks of the kind Anthropic describes, the underlying weakness is an old one: plenty of our gadgets are already easy to commandeer.

BANGKOK — Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh refrained from signaling whether there will be another interest rate hike again this month, while acknowledging a "synchronous tightening" by central banks around the world and there's "no free riders."

"I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year," Warsh said, reiterating his opposition to the use of forward guidance for markets that should rely on interpreting data.

He also acknowledged that stance may disappoint anyone who had hoped for a steer ahead of the central bank meeting later this month. "It's a new chapter at the Fed [and] we're not in that business anymore. But we can go in any direction you'd like," he said.
Warsh spoke at a fireside chat with the International Monetary Fund's managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, as part of the weeklong IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday.
Stock market indexes in Asia and Treasury yields were largely stable following the remarks.

Warsh described the global picture as a common fight on prices. Central banks made their own choices under their own mandates, he said, but the result was "a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world," which means "there's no free riders."
He was more expansive on artificial intelligence, which he called "probably the most consequential change to the U.S. and the global economy in my lifetime."

He expressed optimism about how AI will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, while warning the road there may be "very bumpy," and its near-term effect on jobs is still uncertain.
"I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose," Warsh said. A decade from now, he said, people will look back "and say this was hugely consequential."
The Fed raised rates to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month, its first hike since 2023.

Traders see a 72.3% chance for the Fed to keep the interest rate unchanged at the Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to CME Fed Watch, while the majority expect a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting.
Private equity funds are increasingly pushing their portfolio companies to take on more debt to return cash to their investors, data suggests.
It comes as the typical ways of monetizing private equity investments — selling company stakes via IPOs, or offloading them to other PE funds or buyers — have dried up in recent years.

While investors get paid, the practice of private equity sponsors adding more debt to companies — known as dividend recapitalizations — risks weakening their ability to invest or weather future downturns in trading.

"Dividend recap" activity has surged since 2022, and Moody's Ratings expects it to remain high in Europe, the Middle East and Africa as private equity firms look for ways to return money to investors while company sales and IPOs remain subdued.

The ratings agency estimates that private equity-owned companies in the EMEA region could take on a further 41 billion euros ($46 billion) in debt before reaching leverage levels that typically prompt a downgrade.

New Moody's analysis indicates the practice remains limited to the strongest-performing companies with the greatest capacity to take on new debt, indicating this "significant releveraging capacity" could support a further ramp-up in dividend recaps.
Still, it does not address the exit backlog weighing over private equity, where funds are now having to hold onto companies for much longer than the typical period of around five to six years.

"The fundamental problem is that exits are few and far between – the European IPO markets have been muted, and the capital that would generally fund strategic purchases by large corporates has become a lot more expensive after the last rate hike cycle," said Moody's analyst Mayank Mallik. "Generally, we are more focused on the impact that the general PE ecosystem has on corporate credit quality — and this is one of the key transmission mechanisms currently."
Moody's said PE sponsors have remained "disciplined" in choosing dividend recap candidates, with services, consumer products and manufacturing the most active sectors.

Mallik noted most dividend recaps have involved companies that outperformed their original business plans, with the new debt generally returning leverage to its initial level without "materially" affecting exit opportunities.
"It is true, however, that companies preparing for IPOs like to show a track record of solid deleveraging for a couple of years before approaching the market," he told CNBC via email.

"There is indeed a risk that, if an IPO window unexpectedly opens, issuers that have recently done a div recap may not be able to jump on the opportunity. Any company doing a div-recap is likely taking a forward-looking view that the IPO market will be closed in the short run."

Distributions to investors have fallen sharply in recent years. Moody's, citing PitchBook data, said private equity distributions dropped from more than 30% of starting net asset value in 2022 to about 12% today.
"The risk is that if PE exit backlog is prolonged, sponsors may start looking at relatively weaker credits to monetize, which may lead to credit deterioration across the portfolio," Mallik added.
He said that those risks are greater than a decade ago, partly because documentation has become "quite permissive" for issuers looking to raise additional debt.

Portfolio companies' recaps are typically funded through the broadly syndicated loan market, where several investment banks will club together to lend money to a borrower, thereby spreading the risk. Alternatively, funding is raised by high-yield corporate bond issuance or private credit borrowing.

Sunaina Sinha Haldea, global head of private capital advisory at Raymond James, said there is still "meaningful capacity" to fund recaps, highlighting how tight spreads and scarce new loan supply are helping support appetite.

"Weaker earnings, wider spreads or investor withdrawals could tighten availability, while a recovery in acquisition financing would give lenders more alternatives to funding shareholder payouts," she said.
Haldea noted that dividend recaps provide liquidity, relieving the pressure to sell without ultimately resolving the valuation gap.
"Investors get some cash back, but the asset remains in the fund and still needs an eventual buyer," Haldea told CNBC via email.

"A dividend recap need not derail an exit if earnings growth has created genuine borrowing capacity, but borrowing against hoped-for growth is a different proposition. More debt means less financial flexibility and, at the same enterprise value, less equity value left for shareholders when the business is eventually sold."

Commercial vessels may continue navigating the perilous Strait of Hormuz despite escalating attacks on shipping, as strong demand for Middle Eastern energy and commercial opportunities keep some operators willing to brave the risks, maritime experts said.

The latest attacks on two Singapore-flagged container ships have heightened concerns over the safety of commercial shipping through one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints. But analysts say the incidents are unlikely to bring remaining shipping activity through the Strait to a halt, even as major container lines largely stay away.

Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Singapore's S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said shipping companies were likely to continue seeking opportunities to transit the strait despite heightened security threats.
"I don't see in the short term, that Singapore flagged ships or Singapore shipping companies would necessarily avoid taking the transit if there is an opportunity," Koh told CNBC.

His comments follow attacks on two Singapore-registered container ships, GFS Pride and GFS Giselle, this week. GFS Pride sank after being struck by a projectile and catching fire, while GFS Giselle was damaged. Crew members from both vessels were reported safe.

Crossings through the Strait of Hormuz fell to 131 in the week ended Oct. 14, from 176 the previous week, according to maritime analytics firm Kpler, although the decline cannot be attributed solely to the latest incidents.

Dimitris Ampatzidis, maritime risk and compliance manager at Kpler, said the attacks underscored Iran's continuing ability to threaten commercial vessels, with the risks extending beyond oil and gas transportation.
Koh said shipping companies around the world have continued looking for opportunities to navigate the Strait since the conflict erupted, with some operators prepared to accept higher risks and costs.
Strong demand for oil, particularly from Asia, continues to provide an incentive for tanker operators to transport energy supplies from the Persian Gulf, even as security threats complicate voyages.
Some operators may be willing to take their chances even if doing so involves paying a premium, Koh said.
Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan offered an example of how higher oil prices could make voyages through Hormuz commercially worthwhile despite the dangers.

Speaking at the Milken Institute Asia Summit last week, Balakrishnan recounted a conversation with an unnamed Gulf counterpart who said his country was earning more from oil exports than before the war by operating a so-called "Hormuz shuttle" involving about 20 very large crude carriers.
The vessels were effectively self-insured against attacks, according to the official's account, with higher crude prices making the voyages financially worthwhile despite the risks.
"Sometimes you get hits, but it is still worthwhile to run the 'Hormuz shuttle,'" Balakrishnan quoted the official as saying.
Despite the risks, vessels continue to transit the Strait, reflecting its commercial importance, particularly for energy shipments to Asian markets, Ampatzidis said.
However, further attacks could deter more operators from making the passage, with the impact likely to differ depending on vessel type and individual companies' assessments of the risks, he added.
The Singapore Shipping Association also played down the prospect of a broad withdrawal of commercial shipping from the region, suggesting operators would instead adapt to changing trade conditions.

"Rather than signalling a broad withdrawal from the region, these developments are more likely to result in adjustments to trading patterns as markets respond to shifts in the supply and demand of goods and energy," said association president TS Teo.
Shipowners would continue weighing commercial considerations against security developments and crew safety when making operational decisions, he added.
While some operators remain willing to transit Hormuz, much of the global container shipping industry has already adjusted its networks to avoid the strait.

Jayendu Krishna, a director at Drewry Maritime Advisors, said none of the major container shipping lines had resumed services through Hormuz since suspending operations following the outbreak of the war in February. Only some regional operators have continued sporadic services, generally using smaller feeder vessels.
That means the immediate impact of the latest attacks on container shipping could be limited, he said.

However, a further escalation into the Gulf of Oman could pose a more serious threat to regional supply chains, particularly if it disrupts alternative ports like Khorfakkan in the United Arab Emirates and Oman's Sohar that have become critical gateways for cargo entering Gulf countries.
"If the Gulf of Oman became a zone of kinetic activity, a significant part of supplies to the Gulf countries would be cut off, since Khorfakkan and Sohar have been a lifeline for them," Krishna said.

During a recent interview on the Happy Sad Confused podcast, the actor admitted that while his residual income typically isn’t consistent, he can’t say that about director M. Night Shyamalan‘s 2016 film Split.

“The only one that really consistently pays me is Split,” he told host Josh Horowitz. “Well, I think it was made for like $6 million or something like that. And let’s say they spent $30 [million] advertising it, and in our first weekend, we made $40 [million].”
“So, we were in profit. So our first residual check came at the end of the first weekend. It was bonkers,” McAvoy added.
Split follows three girls who try to escape after being kidnapped by a man (McAvoy) with a diagnosed 23 distinct personalities. He also reprised the role in 2016’s Glass.
The Atonement actor went on to praise Shyamalan, saying he’s “super smart in so many ways.”

“The thing that I took away from him was his preparedness because you know he made that film and Glass on incredibly modest budgets and was very focused,” he said, adding that the filmmaker maximized his shooting time by “being incredibly well-prepared” and “communicat[ing] with the crew.”
While McAvoy has enjoyed the residuals from Split, he also admitted that he doesn’t “get too much money from [2008’s] Wanted.”

“You’ve always got a good back end and there’s some in your contract, you get back end here and back end there. Twenty-three seasons in and Grey’s Anatomy is not going anywhere.

“No one has said anything to me about when the last season of Grey’s is going to be,” showrunner Meg Marinis tells The Hollywood Reporter when chatting about the new season, which returned Thursday night.

That doesn’t mean she doesn’t ask. As the person charged with running ABC‘s long-running, hit medical drama, Marinis wants to be prepared for whenever that day comes. “But it really seems like they want it to be a collaborative decision with Shonda,” she says of show creator Rhimes. “The series has done so much for the studio and network, they [would] want to do it right. And they’re not ready.”

They are in expansion mode, instead. Grey’s, whose previous spinoffs were Private Practice and Station 19, is getting a new spinoff this 2026-2027 season that will be set at a rural West Texas medical center. Marinis co-created and is writing the untitled series with Rhimes, and Grey’s star/executive producer Ellen Pompeo is also exec producing the new show.

“It’s related to Grey’s, but its stories are going to be different,” teases Marinis, who counts Texas as her home state. She’s always wanted to explore “what’s happening in medical deserts,” as well as “the disparity between people who can afford excellent healthcare and the people who can’t.” The latter comes up in the season 23 premiere of Grey’s, “Collide,” which welcomed Pompeo’s Meredith back to the hospital after the season 22 ending that sparked wedding bells for her and Nick (Scott Speedman).

When Grey’s returned, one month had passed since the exits of beloved doctors Teddy (Kim Raver) and Owen (Kevin McKidd), and the episode’s ending sets up more than enough threads to follow in coming weeks. Below, Marinis talks about all of it, including more on the spinoff, how she really feels about medical show competition (we’re looking at you, The Pitt) and how much Pompeo will be on screen this season.

Congrats on the news about the Grey’s spinoff! We know that the series (which doesn’t yet have a name) will premiere sometime in the 2026-2027 season and that it’s set at a rural West Texas medical center — “the last chance for care before miles of nowhere.” You and Grey’s creator Shonda Rhimes are co-creating and writing the show, and Ellen Pompeo is executive producing. How has it been working on this second show amid the Grey’s schedule?
(Laughs.) I have a great team here at Grey’s that I lean on, and Shonda’s doing the new one with me so it’s easier when there’s two of us!
Where are you in your work on the spinoff? Is there a timeline?

We are working away. I can’t say much, but we’re far enough along where I’m really, really excited. We’re digging into the actual communities and true stories of what happens out in rural West Texas. There’s so much going on there that I haven’t seen on TV. I’m thrilled to be able to dive into that world. It’s so different from Grey’s. It’s related to Grey’s, but its stories are going to be different.
Previous Grey’s spinoffs were Private Practice and Station 19, but this feels a world away from Grey’s‘ Seattle hospital. Were there lessons learned from those two shows that you are applying now?

The only lessons are good lessons from those two. They were very successful spinoffs with hardcore fan followings. I loved both of them. This one is something dear to my heart [Marinis is from Houston, Texas] and being on a medical show like Grey’s, and hearing a lot about what’s happening in medical deserts, it’s hard to show that in Seattle. I’ve always been really interested in showing it, and in doing a small town show in Texas.
Will Grey’s launch the Texas show in-show this season?

We have thoughts based on airing schedule and things like that, but we’re still working it out, also because there are so many things going on on Grey’s, I want to make sure to do it where it’s servicing both shows equally.
How do you view this within the larger Grey’s franchise? Does it signal anything about the flagship?

It’s just expanding the flagship. No one has said anything to me about when the last season of Grey’s is going to be. I think it’s never! I always ask and they’re like, “Not now!” You always want to be prepared, as a showrunner of a season 23 show, that you’re aware of when that decision is going to happen. But it really seems like they want it to be a collaborative decision with Shonda. Because the series has done so much for the studio network, they want to do it right. And they’re not ready.

We last spoke after last season’s finale and the exits of Kim Raver and Kevin McKidd’s Teddy and Owen, respectively, which you said was a difficult decision and related to the budget, which is something shows are experiencing across the industry. How did you approach season 23 with your very large ensemble? Will there be characters we see more or less of? Are you still feeling those constraints?

Not yet. I mean, you always feel the general constraints of a large ensemble and what’s going on in the industry, so I’m mindful of how many times we go out on location and things like that. So the general constraints, yes. But no, those conversations usually are when they approach me later in the season — to drop that news on me!

We’re in a positive place right now. On the show, the hospital is having some budget issues as well, but that’s mainly continuing on what we started last year about what’s happening to research funding and funding for healthcare in general. Now Grey Sloan is just feeling more of it.
How much time has passed since the finale to start this premiere, and how is the hospital rebounding from losing veteran doctors, Teddy and Owen?

It’s been about a month. We did that for a couple of reasons. I’ve done direct pickups for the past couple of seasons and I wanted to do something different, to start stories in different places. Also, I didn’t have Nick [Scott Speedman] available to me at the beginning of this season — he was left in the hospital in the finale, and he was busy on [his ABC show] R.J. Decker. That played into the decision. And I really wanted time for this VIP floor to come into play. We didn’t see that floor when we left the season last year.

We don’t mention Teddy and Owen a ton in the premiere, because it’s been a month, and I didn’t want to start on such a down note. But we’re definitely feeling, and I’m feeling, the loss of Teddy and Owen. I’m searching for them in the scripts. We have to get a new chief. We don’t have a head of trauma right now. And it’s just leading to how busy the hospital is, maybe how our ER is not functioning as well as it should be. Winston [Anthony Hill] can do what he can, but he’s not a military trauma surgeon.
James Wolk is a new character who was announced with a four-episode arc. Now we know his role — he’s the new chief. Will that arc extend? And how extensive was your search for the new chief?

I love having him, but, you know, chiefs can come and go quickly on this show! But he’s a great character. He’s very fun to write for. He is also just a delightful human being and he seems to really enjoy his time here. We always have a long list of options [of actors] that people are sending us. He fit that suave look we wanted. He really seems like a villain you learn to love. Even when he’s being snarky about money, he’s still fascinating to watch.

You say you got a long list of actors who want to come and play on Grey’s, a network show in its 23rd season. How does that make you feel as showrunner about how appealing the show still is in the streaming era?

It makes me feel great. I credit it to our show filming in L.A. If you have your family here, it’s really appealing to get to do an arc in L.A. I think there’s a reason we’re in season 23. It works, and I think a lot of people are fans of the show and curious about the show because it’s been going on for so long. And also, we’re really nice over here! People tell me all the time. Guest actors will write me emails and say, “This is the nicest set I’ve ever been on.”

This episode had a line that Debbie Allen’s Catherine said to Ellen Pompeo, when she tells Meredith about hiring a new chief, “Well, you’re not here all the time” — which also could apply to Pompeo’s lesser onscreen role. Did those two have fun doing that scene?

Yeah, they really enjoyed it! Sometimes we write stuff like that and we don’t even really think about it, and then when you watch it on set, you’re like, “I didn’t mean it that way!” (Laughs.) But you know Debbie threw some sass into it and they were they were laughing; the two of them together laughed really hard.
How much will we see Ellen Pompeo on screen this season? I ask you every year, but is it more or less? The same? [Pompeo is also working as an EP on the Texas spinoff.]

Like I say, every year, we take her as much as we can get. I know she has a couple of things going on in the mix, but we’re scheduling around that and she really lets me know ahead of time the days she is around, and it’s the same thing with Scott [Speedman]. It’s a logistics game, right? You want everybody to be able to do all their other projects, because work is work and it’s important right now to keep working in the industry. She and I have a good relationship. We’ll plan things out, and I’m more than happy to schedule around her.
Will you be building towards Meredith and Nick’s wedding this season?
We will definitely see Scott later in the season. In the premiere, we couldn’t work it out. But we’ll see Scott and we’ll definitely tag that engagement.
So engagement, but you’re not confirming a wedding this season…

Meredith’s storyline in this premiere highlights the upstairs-downstairs of Grey Sloan. Meredith is fighting back against tiered treatment and Catherine is approaching this as a plan to help with their financials. How is this a larger story you want to tell this season, and why did that interest Ellen for this to be Meredith’s fight, at least for now?

I’m interested in telling that story because I’m seeing it so much now across healthcare. The disparity is growing even wider between people who can afford excellent healthcare and the people who can’t. I think it’s also really interesting because, historically, Grey Sloan has always provided VIP care, the way we’ve told it on the show. So now, are they dividing care into tiers? A lot of our doctors are going to question it.

But these floors are popping up all over the country. Obviously, they’ve had them in L.A. for a while, but also in New York, and even when I went to see my dad and Houston. When he had pneumonia, there was a VIP floor there. I saw the signs and I was like, “What’s the difference between what my dad’s getting and what they’re getting?” I find it fascinating.

There are a lot of stories where sometimes you don’t want to be on the VIP floor because they don’t have all the tools you need if something catastrophic happens. But also, if I had a very chronically ill family member and I had the means, why wouldn’t I throw every dollar I had at helping? It’s an interesting debate to sink our teeth into.

Meredith, especially, is an owner of the hospital, so she understands the business. But her whole career, she has fought for the have-nots. So it’s like, do you keep the hospital doors open? What side do you choose?
Will Ellen be appearing in batches, like a five-episode arc to tell storylines? Or will she pop in and out in a less structured way?
I would love for it to be structured like that, but schedules aren’t working! (Laughs.) But there are runs where she’s in for more than one episode.
Do you have an episode count for her this season?
Are there any other returns you can tease?
Probably not. Obviously, she’s been in the picture, so people know that Jen Landon is returning [as Toni]. But as for old cast series regulars, I can’t tease any of that right now.

The Grey’s social account teased a Cristina Yang (Sandra Oh) return, and the fans went wild. They were speculating Yang would maybe come back for Meredith’s wedding to Nick. Anything you can say about that?
She is welcome to walk in these doors anytime! I would love for her to. At one point, she was doing some theater in London, but it would be a dream come true to have her back.

You also kicked this season off with a classic disaster episode, and one that picks up on a lot of relationship threads that were unfinished at the end of last season, taking a backseat to Teddy and Owen’s big goodbye. Did this premiere feel more nostalgic to you — chaos and romance?

You’re right that a lot of stories had to take up smaller real estate in the last couple of episodes at the end of last season, rightfully so, because we were writing off two long-term, beloved characters. I love when people have relationship issues with each other, and you have to throw them on a medical case together. There’s nothing more Grey’s than that. I love all those looks between Amelia and Toni and them having to come together; and Simone [Alexis Floyd] and Lucas [Niko Terho] and West [Trevor Jackson]; Jules [Adelaide Kane] and Winston having to operate with Bailey (Chandra Wilson). It’s quintessential Grey’s when there’s the bubbling underneath it as they’re trying to save someone’s life.
You have a pregnancy reveal at the end of this premiere with Simone.
Grey’s has tackled pregnancy and abortion storylines before. How will this one be different?

It is different. We’ve never done it this way before. It’s going to take a couple of episodes to play out. I also think this one is different because Simone was just told that she probably wouldn’t be able to have children; to be able to conceive and get pregnant. So that’s going to be top of mind for her. That’s a struggle. She’s someone who’s put career first and she’s worked really hard to get where she is. I think that’s what a lot of us struggle with, right? Do you put the career on pause for a second and start a family? It’s something so many people relate to, so we’ll show that. But it is different. We’ve never done it this way before.
The other bomb at the end of the premiere is Jo (Camilla Luddington) quitting the hospital, as Link (Chris Carmack) is still being secretive about his pills. This couple is always tested!

I know, what can I do? I love torturing them! Sometimes they’ll be like, “Really?!” They have such talent to play funny stories, and we played them very light and funny for a long time. Then I kind of tapped into this talent that I did not know they both had, and it’s amazing to watch. Their performances are so great. Even Jo watching that thing in the elevator? Camilla’s performance is exquisite. So yeah — we’re putting them through it again. (Laughs.)

Blue got fired at the end of last season, and now Harry Shum Jr. is on Dancing With the Stars. Did he come to you for approval to be on that series, and is that impacting his story and all? Obviously, he’s back as a series regular.

It did not impact his story. It just happened to be that he was the character who was quitting, and then he, ABC and his team came to me after and I was like, “Oh, this really worked out, because now people are going to think once he’s announced on DWTS that maybe we went through with [firing him off the show].” But I think there’s been so much social media of him in his scrubs that his return is spoiled!

We’re so happy for him. He’s so talented. A lot of us have gotten to go see the live taping of DWTS. You’ll see him and Jenna Johnson just rehearsing outside in between setups for Grey’s. On Tuesdays, Harry’s not here because Dancing With the Stars films. But other than Tuesdays, he’s really been able to schedule rehearsals around the show. I’m sure he’s exhausted!

Grey’s remains the longest-running medical drama on TV. But more medical shows are popping up on streaming; there’s The Pitt. You could compare that to ER, which was on at the beginning of Grey’s. Does that sharpen what you’re trying to do? Do you ever worry about overlap? How do you feel about medical show competition?

I don’t worry too much about it because I feel like what’s good for one medical show is good for all. It’s trending again. Anytime that it can trend, I think it’s a great thing. We’re so different than The Pitt that I don’t worry about that one. I was a huge ER fan. It had a huge influence on me wanting to be a TV writer. I love medical shows. I love the better ones more. (Laughs.) And then I’m excited to introduce this new [the Texas spinoff] into the fold.
Grey’s is a streaming show too now, on Netflix, courting new generations of viewers. But 23 seasons in, what are your tricks to keeping the show fresh and keeping the cast engaged?

It has been a long time and it can be difficult. It can be tricky, but I also think that medicine has changed so much and the world has changed so much. Between AI and climate change and where money goes toward research, there are always new things that we haven’t explored. Often, we have an overwhelming amount of stories we want to tell and we don’t get to tell all of them, so we have a huge bank of things we’re interested in. Also, knowing that we have a 23-year history of characters who have come and gone and bringing them back. And, you can always introduce new interns!
You have three series originals stars who are still on the show: Ellen, Chandra Wilson and James Pickens Jr. Are you never letting them go?
Yes, I will say, I am never letting those three go! I mean, I hope they never go. It’s not gonna be me who writes it!

Twisters has had a lasting impact on Daisy Edgar-Jones, but not necessarily in the way that she wanted.

During a recent episode of Jake Shane‘s Therapuss podcast, the actress revealed that she might be “slightly deaf” in one ear after shooting the 2024 action-adventure thriller, directed by Lee Isaac Chung.

“I think I still am slightly deaf in my left ear because there was so much debris and wind that was entering from a sharp left,” she said. “It was a windy shoot. It was quite ironic because we were shooting in Oklahoma and often would have to shut down filming because of an actual wind storm, to then recreate a wind storm once it’s passed. It was a wild experience.”

Twisters, which served as a standalone sequel, came nearly two decades after 1996’s Twister. The film followed Kate Carter (Edgar-Jones), a retired tornado-chaser and meteorologist who is persuaded to return to Oklahoma to work with a new team and new technologies. There, she meets Tyler Owens (played by Glen Powell), a content creator who posts his storm-chasing adventures.
The Sense and Sensibility star definitely wasn’t afraid to get in on the action, previously telling The Hollywood Reporter that she got “a bit addicted” to doing stunts after filming Twisters.

“It was so stunt heavy and I’d never done really proper stunts, so I was so curious to see how they were going to achieve a lot of the action sequences, but I’m a bit addicted now, I’ve got the bug,” Edgar-Jones said in 2024. “It was so much fun. The release of a new Avalanches album is never a trifling matter.

With their debut 2000 album Since I Left You, the Australian electronic act let loose into the world a masterpiece. A peerless, timeless work, its creators meticulously sewed thousands of vinyl samples from the likes of Françoise Hardy, Sérgio Mendes, Raekwon, Wayne and Shuster, and even Madonna.
Fast-forward a quarter century, Since I Left You sits in a class of all-time classics. Fresh as a field of daisies.
Then, the “difficult second album.” The Avalanches recorded and rejected the followup. Years went by without a peep, save for the score to the King Kong stage musical and a batch of remixes.
When their full-length sophomore collecting Wildflower finally bloomed, 16 long years had passed. Wildflower went straight to No. 1 on the ARIA Albums Chart.
A third album travelled at comparative light-speed in 2020, We Will Always Love You, and later scooped the coveted Australian Music Prize, for the best album of the year.

Now led by Robbie Chater, Tony Di Blasi and Andy Szekere, The Avalanches rumble on with their fourth studio effort No Bad Memories. It’s an album stacked with tracks (31 of them) and guests, including Karen O, John Glacier, Jamie xx, Barry Can’t Swim, Rivers Cuomo and Mike Patton.

No Bad Memories (via Modular Recordings/Universal) explores “the magical intersection of advertising, memory and nostalgia,” reads a statement accompanying the project, “examining how jingles, sonic logos, commercials and the sounds of technology quietly embed themselves in our lives, becoming inseparable from the memories they soundtrack.”
Sonically, it’s a joy. With bounce and soul. The Avalanches manage to harness the energy of a litter of Pomeranians.

“Our album No Bad Memories is out in the world today,” reads a statement from the act. “We’re beyond grateful for the endless enthusiasm and love our music receives after all this time. Thank you for taking the time to listen, we hope you enjoy it.”

Timing out at 52 minutes, No Bad Memories is accompanied by a music video for “I Give Everything I Have 2 U” featuring Loaded Honey. Haley Joel Osment stars in the visual, shot by cinematographer Andrés Arochi (Long Legs) on location in Tokyo.

“Working with our friend Haley on the visual for this song was such a thrill,” The Avalanches say of the Sixth Sense actor. “A one-take scenario with Haley trying to navigate the Shibuya traffic, a huge camera strapped to the outside of his windshield is not a bad memory indeed!”
Avalanches dates are coming up in the United States, Continental Europe, the United Kingdom and Asia, followed by a tour of Australia in early 2027.

Oct. 16 (UPI) -- Three people were killed and more than a dozen others were injured Thursday when a bus involved in a multivehicle crash erupted into flames in western Canada, authorities said.
A total of 16 people were injured, including a police officer who responded to the scene, authorities said during a press conference.
Of those injured, 10 were transported to local hospitals, one in critical condition and nine with non-life-threatening injuries.
Five others were classified as "walking wounded," meaning they were cleared at the scene but taken to the hospital for further assessment, authorities said.
Calgary Police Service Staff Sgt. Andy Woodward told reporters that the incident occurred at about 1 p.m. MDT in northeastern Calgary.

He said a city bus collided with a white car that then crashed into other vehicles. The bus continued through an intersection and hit a city bus parked at a bus stop, causing the second bus to erupt into flames.
That second bus then crashed into additional vehicles.
At least eight vehicles were involved in the crash, according to authorities, who said the cause of the incident remains under investigation.
The second bus was powered by natural gas, which authorities said was believed to be the cause of the explosion and the subsequent fire.
"I've worked as a police officer for 36 years and I think this is probably the biggest scene that I've worked on," he said.
Calgary Fire Department Chief Steve Dongworth told reporters that the incident occurred close to a fire house and that the blaze was "a relatively quick knockdown."
Because of the threat posed by the natural gas, the hazardous materials unit was called to the scene, he added.
"It was fairly involved. It wasn't a catastrophic fire, but it was a serious fire inside, particularly the liquid natural gas bus," he said, stating there was also a small fire in the initial bus.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney offered his sympathies to those affected by the crash online.
"To the families enduring this heartbreaking loss, to those recovering and to everyone grieving in the community, know that Canadians are holding you close in our hearts," he said in a statement.

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 15 (UPI) -- Street Fighter, in theaters Friday, is a fun live-action video game. The film celebrates the cartoonish absurdity of the game, though it exposes the limits of modern filmmaking while at it.
In 1987, Ryu (Andrew Koji) won the World Warrior Tournament. Then his master was murdered, so Ryu disappeared.
Even his best friend, Ken Masters (Noah Centineo), doesn't know where Ryu is. Ken became a popular fighter with endorsements and MTV promos.

When M. Bison (David Dastmalchian) puts on the second ever World Warrior Tournament in 1993, he invites Ken to lure Ryu. BIson has been trying to siphon off the psycho power of world class fighters but only Ryu has enough Hadouken for Bison.

If it weren't clear before, the mention of psycho power clarifies that Street Fighter knows what it is. Director Kitao Sakurai, with a script he wrote with T.J. Fixman and Dalan Musson, is not trying to explore the serious dramatic heft of the Street Fighter mythology.
These are beloved characters, and the film celebrates them. But, it celebrates them by having fun with them, not slavishly depicting the canon of the Capcom fighting game series.

All of the fight scenes are choreographed to accommodate the characters' special moves from the games. There may be some bona fide martial arts in between, but the point of the game was to use fighting moves that could not exist in real life. That's why it was fun to play.

There are plenty of real martial arts movies. There are far fewer live-action video game movies and even fewer of them are any good. So depicting Honda's (Hirooki Goto) Hundred Hand Slap and Dhalsim's (Vidyut Jammwal) Yoga Lance is unique.

This is also the first live-action Street Fighter movie that is actually about a fighting tournament. The previous two incorporated fights in their plots, but this one weaves a plot around the tournament.
Some of the characters get eliminated off-screen, but the film finds room for each character to have their moment.

Unfortunately, the main combat arena looks like a typically artificial screen environment. Whether green screen or LED, it's clear none of the fights were filmed in front of an actual live audience of extras.
Too many other scenes take place in dark chambers. Street Fighter is a colorful game. The film's costumes are good, at least.
At times, it tries too hard to be campy, from Ken's diva celebrity behavior to Bison's pseudo-wisdom. The 1994 Street Fighter was campy because of its sincere commitment to its own absurdity.
Dastmalchian even repeats the best line from Raul Julia's Bison in the 1994 Street Fighter, because it has become an internet meme more famous than the film from which it was derived.

Setting the film in 1993 comes with fun pop culture references and needle drops of the era. "Black Hole Sun," "Too Legit to Quit" and "Come Out and Play" are choice tracks. Although Meredith Brooks came later, her inclusion is fun too.

Oct. 15 (UPI) -- Three children, a teacher and a suspected gunman are dead following a shooting Thursday afternoon at an Oregon elementary school, authorities said.
Police identified the suspected shooter as a 16-year-old resident of Bend, a city of nearly 100,000 people in central Oregon, located about 130 miles east of Eugene.
Authorities said the shooting occurred at about 1 p.m. PDT at Silver Rail Elementary School.

The deceased victims have been identified only as children ages 5, 8, and 11, and a teacher. A 7-year-old student and a 54-year-old teacher were injured in the shooting and were transported to St. Charles Bend Medical Center with critical injuries, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told reporters during a press conference.
"This is a terrible tragedy and we are working hard to investigate this incident and get as much information as possible out to the public," Krantz said.
Dispatch received its first call about the incident at 12:59 p.m. from a person in a vehicle who said they had been shot at multiple times by a suspect with a long gun.

Dozens of calls followed, reporting that a shooter had entered the school, with the first responding officers arriving at the scene at 1:02 p.m., a minute after the school was directed to enter lockdown.
Moments after police arrived, an officer reported that the suspect had been shot by a community member who had witnessed the suspect enter the school and pursued the gunman.
Officers then entered the building and confirmed the suspect was dead, evacuated the facility and rendered emergency aid to those injured, Krantz said.
Including the shooter, five people were found dead at the scene, he said, adding that the families of the victims have been notified.
All students and staff evacuated from the school were transported to a local church used as a reunification site, authorities said.

"In August, every Bend police officer went through a full day of threat training at a local high school. And unfortunately, this is something we train for on a regular basis and we must," Krantz said.
The ensuing investigation will be lengthy, he said, adding that there will be a large police presence at the school for the next couple of days.
The website for Bend-La Pine Schools, the district that operates Silver Rail Elementary, states all schools will be closed Friday.

"This is something we never want to happen anywhere, but especially and particularly in our beautiful community here in Bend. There are not really any words that I can say to any of you that will make this better, but please know we are working hard to ensure we conduct a thorough investigation," Krantz said.

A preliminary investigation indicates the shooter gained access to the school by firing the long gun at locked doors, Krantz said, though he would not identify what specific weapon the suspect used nor how many shots were fired in the shooting.
It was also unknown at the time of the press conference what weapon was used by the member of the public who shot the suspected shooter or how many shots they had fired.

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek, a progressive Democrat, thanked Silver Rail Elementary staff, parents and first responders who rushed to the scene. She also expressed gratitude toward the unidentified community member who engaged the suspected shooter, saying they "heroically intervened to save further loss of life."
"Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," she said.
She said all Oregonians mourn the shooting.

"This is a horrible day. No parent should have to have this kind of day and no community should have to live through this kind of day. And as we learn more about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured and their families and their loved ones we are going to do a lot of crying and we are going to cry together and we're probably going to cry privately," she said.
"We must come together and support each other, neighbor to neighbor, Oregonian to Oregonian."
