Every four years, February gets an extra day. You’ve heard of these “leap” years, especially if an acquaintance was born on the unusual date of February 29. What you might not have heard of, however, is the leap year’s sporadic sibling: the leap second.

This lesser-known timekeeping fix was center stage at this week’s General Conference on Weights and Measures in France, where timekeepers decided today to return it to obscurity by getting rid of it altogether.

Traditionally, one Earth orbit around the sun determines the length of a year, and one Earth rotation on its axis determines the length of a day. Because it takes Earth around 365.25 days to go around the sun, timekeepers add that extra leap day once every four years to make sure our seasonal calendar stays aligned with the orbit.

Earth’s daily rotation, however, isn’t as regular, because the speed of the planet’s spin can change. In general, Earth’s rotational speed has been slowing down throughout history. But starting around 2020, it has increased. A number of factors can play a role in Earth’s spin, including the atmosphere, ocean currents, wind, volcanoes and melting polar ice.
This makes Earth’s rotation a “lousy” clock, Jeff Sherman, a physicist at the United States’ National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), tells CNN’s Katie Hunt.
Earth’s rotation does not exactly match the length of a day on our clocks. Right now, the average day on Earth is slightly longer than 24 hours. October 14, 2026, was 24 hours and 0.0006471 seconds.

Even as Earth’s spin wavers, our atomic clocks—crucial to keeping ultra-precise time in this age of computers, phones, GPS and satellites—tick at a stable rate. That’s because in 1967, the General Conference on Weights and Measures chose a reliable way to define a second with the help of the isotope cesium-133. When a cesium-133 atom undergoes a change between specific energy states, it emits radiation that oscillates in an exceptionally regular manner, Vahe Peroomian, a physicist at the University of Southern California, writes for the Conversation. As such, scientists reclassified a second as equivalent to 9,192,631,770 cesium-133 atom oscillations.

Today, Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) follows this principal. But astronomical time, or Universal Time 1 (UT1), follows Earth’s fickle rotation, sometimes leading to discrepancies between the two time scales. To keep these systems as aligned as possible, timekeepers have added 27 leap seconds to UTC since 1972. “We effectively stop our clocks for that second to give Earth the opportunity to catch up,” as Konstantin Bikos and Anne Buckle write for Time and Date.

The goal has been for UTC and UT1 to differ by less than 0.9 seconds, and a leap second has been added when the misalignment approaches that limit. Today, however, experts at the General Conference on Weights and Measures voted to increase this margin to one hour. This negates the need for a leap second and creates the much rarer leap hour, which will be added when UTC deviates from UT1 by 3,600 seconds. Such a change likely won’t be needed for hundreds or thousands of years.

“It’s kind of a philosophical discussion, because if a leap hour happens, it won’t be for a very, very long time,” Christian Bizouard, director of the IERS Earth Orientation Center in France, tells the Guardian’s Ian Sample. “What we are doing is pushing back the decision.”

The move caps off 30 years of debate, as the leap second has been highly controversial in the world of timekeeping. Leap seconds aren’t nearly as smooth of a fix as leap years are, and they can cause computer and website issues. Reddit famously crashed when a leap second was added on June 30, 2012. It’s “always been a problem,” Judah Levine, a former researcher at the NIST’s Time and Frequency Division, tells Scientific American’s Emma Gometz.

Instead of adding the entire second all at once, companies such as Google and Meta add the extra time in smaller segments in a tactic called “smearing,” according to the Conversation. It’s not a simple task, however, and companies that employ smearing have long lobbied to get rid of the leap second.

What’s more, with Earth’s recent spin acceleration, timekeepers around the world were facing the possibility of the world’s first negative leap second, in which a second would be subtracted from UTC. This sparked fears, akin to those surrounding Y2K, that our modern technologies wouldn’t be able to handle such a change.

“It’s never happened before, and therefore the software for that has never been tested,” Darryl Veitch, a researcher who leads the Timing Lab at the University of Technology Sydney, tells the Australian Broadcasting Corporation’s Ellen Phiddian. But others argued that it wouldn’t be much of a problem.
The vote means that in the future, UTC will be allowed to diverge from astronomical time more than ever before.

“Astronomers, Earth scientists and other users of Earth-orientation data will need to account for the growing offset when relating their observations and measurements to civil time,” Peroomian writes in the Conversation. As for everyone else, hopefully whatever technology rules everyday life when a leap hour does eventually come around will be better equipped for the time fix.

Just outside of Paris, perched on an island in the Seine River, a massive, much-anticipated institution is preparing to open its doors. Spanning some 54,000 square feet, the capital region’s newest contemporary art center, which officially debuts this weekend, appears poised to live up to its name: Large.

The scale of the new development on Île Seguin is, in fact, large. Shining with a copper and aluminum exterior, Large is the centerpiece of a roughly 570,000-square-foot, $500-million development called Pointe des Arts, which includes a performing arts center, movie theater, sculpture garden, hotel, shopping district and more.
Though Large’s name is also meant to evoke the French phrase “prendre le large,” which means “to set sail,” the island it sits on is better known among Parisians for its rich automotive history.

Throughout much of the 20th century, the island belonging to the inner suburb of Boulogne-Billancourt was home to the original Renault car factory, an industrial and economic powerhouse for France. In the 1930s, more than 30,000 workers made their living at the plant. But after its closure in 1992, the island began to stall. The abandoned plant was not torn down until 2005, and the effort to turn the post-industrial site into a public space moved slowly.
- Renault company founder Louis Renault continued to produce vehicles under the German occupation of France in World War II, leading to his postwar arrest for collaboration.
- The Renault company was subsequently nationalized in 1945.

“In the face of trials and tribulations, the project called for a great deal of perseverance,” Pierre-Christophe Baguet, the mayor of Boulogne-Billancourt, says in a statement. “Over the course of almost 20 years, many succumbed to fatalism and discouragement and gave up on the site. Others sought to derail the project rather than to see it succeed. … It is a great victory over ignorance and prevailing selfishness.”

As an homage to the location’s history, Large’s inaugural exhibition, titled “Imaginary Engine,” will focus on the relationship between humans and machines, with a particular emphasis on cars. The show features more than 100 artworks created by 55 artists from 23 countries. The oldest pieces on display were made in the 1930s, while 17 pieces were commissioned for the museum’s opening.

“Opening a new institution is always rare, and doing it on an island so charged with memory is a real privilege,” Cecilia Alemani, who curated “Imaginary Engine,” tells ARTnews’ Sarah Belmont. “The Renault factory was dismantled long ago, and today a brand-new building rises in its place, open to everyone.”

The exhibition is separated into five thematic chapters, each exploring industrial constraints and mechanical language with a variety of media. Accompanying the exhibition, which runs through March 7, is a series of film screenings that center iconic cars and car chases, including The Blues Brothers, Thelma and Louise and Taxi Tehran.

Starting with “Imaginary Engines,” Large is meant to serve a similar function to the Museum of Modern Art in New York City. “Paris needed a place where it could showcase art by artists who live and work here, whether they are established or emerging,” Paula Aisemberg, Large’s director, tells the New York Times’ Tina Isaac-Goizé.
Large plans to operate by rotating temporary exhibitions throughout its vast public-facing space, 40 percent of which will cost nothing to visit. Visitors who are 26 or younger will be admitted free.

“‘Large’ is its name. It is an invitation to set sail, to shift our perspectives, and to broaden our horizons,” Laurent Dumas, president of Large, says in the statement. “Because art transforms our ways of seeing and understanding the world, it is essential that we share and transmit it.”
“Imaginary Engine” will be on view at Large in Boulogne-Billancourt, France, from October 17, 2026, to March 7, 2027.

The day the boy found the diary, he’d been scrounging for treasures at the local dump in Stourbridge, England. He and his friends had entered through a small opening at the bottom of a wire fence. Then they spotted something among the bottles and cans: a nearly four-inch-long volume with a green cover, its pages turning in the wind.

The year was 1965, but the diary entries dated to 1918. Their author was a man named Corporal Claude Nuttall, who had served as an infantryman (or “Digger”) in the Australian Army during World War I. He met his wife, Violet Palfreyman, while recovering from an injury in an English hospital. Weeks after the wedding, he returned to the front.

Did Nuttall ever make it home? The boy wondered about the soldier’s fate, and the diary offered several ominous clues. The corner appeared to have been pierced by a bullet, and its pages were stained with blood. Nuttall’s last entry was dated August 10, 1918. The pages that followed were blank.
“Heavy bombardment by our guns. Push still in progress,” he wrote. “Packed up ready to move forward again. Prisoners still coming back. Wrote to Violet.”

The diary eventually made its way to Colin Reid, a former curator at the Dudley Museum and Art Gallery in England’s West Midlands, who spent decades researching the soldier’s story. The culmination of his efforts is the book The Digger’s Diary, which comes out this fall.

“At the start, I wanted to solve the mystery of Claude’s fate,” Reid tells Smithsonian magazine. “An emotional compulsion, I suppose. The fact that his diary was unfinished, bloodstained and had been punctured by a bullet compelled me to find out if he had survived and returned back to Violet.”

The story of the diary’s discovery begins with the Stourbridge dump. The boy who found the volume was 12-year-old Alan Southall, who held onto it for three decades. In 1996, he showed up at the Dudley Museum asking for Reid, who was then working on a World War I exhibition. Southall pulled out the diary, which he’d carefully tucked inside a plastic bag, and asked whether the curator wanted to put it on display.

But Southall had other questions, too. In The Digger’s Diary, the curator recalls what his visitor told him: “For 30 years, I’ve wanted to know Corporal Nuttall’s fate. But I have never done anything about it, because I don’t think things ended well for him.”

The diary went on view in the museum’s exhibition, titled “The Great War.” But when the show closed, Reid kept thinking about the little book with the green cover. About a decade later, he decided to write a book of his own. The curator tracked down Southall, who let him borrow the diary.

Reid got to work, searching for any information he could find about the Australian soldier. “The more I learned, the more I wanted to learn,” he tells BBC News’ Aida Fofana and Sarah Julian. “Right from the very first moment that I held the diary, I had that real sense of connection with it. I was really hooked.”
- On August 4, 1914, Australia entered World War I—the deadliest conflict in the country’s history.
- According to the Australian War Memorial, the country’s population was fewer than five million at the time, and the death toll was more than 60,000.

Born in 1895, Nuttall enlisted in the Australian Army’s 23rd Battalion in 1915, just after his 20th birthday. He traveled to the Western Front, where he fought the Germans. In his diary, he’d written that he’d been awarded a medal from George V; Reid had always wanted to know more about the courageous act that merited this reward. He found the answer in Nuttall’s military records: On his 21st birthday, in July 1916, the soldier had helped rescue injured soldiers from no man’s land, the perilous stretch of earth between opposing trenches.

Later that year, Nuttall was wounded in northern France. He was sent to a hospital in Stourbridge, where he met Palfreyman. The couple tied the knot in March 1918. “All excited,” the corporal wrote in his journal. “Married 12:30 p.m. All went well.” Five weeks later, he shipped out again. His service records show that he died on August 13, 1918, just three days after his final diary entry.

Thanks to Palfreyman’s relatives, Reid tracked down photos from the couple’s wedding. He also traveled to Cheltenham, the Australian suburb where the soldier grew up, to meet Nuttall’s family, as well as the French battlefields where Nuttall had fought and died.

In 2018, Reid and Southall met up with Arthur Thomas, the corporal’s nephew, to visit Nuttall’s grave in Harbonnieres, France. Together, they commemorated the 100th anniversary of his death. A few months later, the diary was returned to Nuttall’s family at a ceremony in Cheltenham.

“I keep saying that the saddest part is that my mother, her two sisters and even Claude’s own mother know nothing of this. I can’t tell them what’s happened,” Thomas told the Dudley News’ Kelly Harris in 2018. “I have seen pictures of Claude’s wedding and Violet’s family that they would never have seen.”

But what about the bloodstains? Was the bullet that struck the diary fatal? “I’m afraid that I can’t reveal that to you,” Reid tells Smithsonian. “It’s a huge spoiler, and the emotional climax of the book—definitely embargoed.”

He can, however, reveal Palfreyman’s fate, which was equally tragic. After Nuttall’s death, she married the owner of a carpet shop. The couple had a son named Eric and a baby girl who died soon after she was born. Palfreyman herself died from childbirth complications a few months later. “She and the child are buried together at Holy Trinity Church in Stourbridge,” Reid says, “barely 100 yards from the altar where she and Claude were married.”

The Digger’s Diary, as the author writes in the preface, is a “tribute to the man I discovered: a forgotten hero, a soldier of quiet fortitude and extraordinary courage.” But it’s also a tribute to the woman Nuttall fell in love with—and to Reid’s own wife, who shares her name. The book begins with a dedication page, which reads simply “For Violet.”
While working on his land in a village in northern Egypt, a man made an astonishing discovery: the remains of two massive statues of Ramesses II.

The man, Khaled el-Shahat, immediately notified the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, which sent a team to the village of Behbeit El Hagar to excavate and study the statues, the ministry said in a translated statement.

Ramesses II had one of the longest reigns in Egypt's history, ruling from around 1279 to 1213 B.C. During his 66 years in power, Egypt controlled an empire that stretched as far northeast as modern-day Syria. He initiated many building projects throughout the empire, and numerous Ramesses II statues have been found throughout Egypt.

Archaeologists had previously found architectural fragments bearing the name of Ramesses II at Behbeit El Hagar, which is known for its temple dedicated to Isis, a goddess associated with healing and magic, said Mahmoud Emam, an Egyptologist at Cairo University who has worked on remains from the site but was not involved with the recent excavation. He noted that the newly found statues were unearthed on the western side of the temple complex.

Both of the newfound statues were once larger than life, with the bigger one likely standing nearly 28 feet (8.5 meters) tall when it was originally built. However, most of what remains is its head, which is 5.2 feet (1.6 m) tall and depicts the pharaoh wearing the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt.

Part of this large statue's back pillar has a hieroglyphic inscription that gives the pharaoh's "Horus" name: Hor-Ka-Nakht-Mery-Maat. This name means "Strong Bull, Beloved of Right, Truth," Joyce Tyldesley, a professor emeritus of Egyptology at the University of Manchester in the U.K., wrote in her book "Ramesses: Egypt's Greatest Pharaoh" (Penguin Books, 2001). In Egypt, it was common for pharaohs to have several alternate names with a Horus name, given in honor of the sky god Horus.

The second statue, which stands about 7.9 feet (2.4 m), also likely depicts Ramesses II, the statement said. The king is shown wearing the "Nemes" headdress, a type of striped headcloth that pharaohs wore, the Egypt Exploration Society notes on its website.

Near this statue is a block of pink granite with two hieroglyphic inscriptions that name Ramesses II and describe him as "King of Upper and Lower Egypt" and the "Son of Ra," an ancient Egyptian sun god, the statement said.
The new finds add more evidence that Ramesses II was heavily invested in the site.

Previous discoveries include two architectural fragments bearing the name of Ramesses II near the Isis temple at Behbeit El Hagar, Emam and his colleagues reported in a 2017 paper. One is believed to be from the upper part of a statue, and another seems to originate from the upper part of a wall.

"We concluded that Ramesses II had undertaken major building works at the temple and recommended further archaeological investigations to shed more light on the early history of the site," Emam said. He noted that the site is threatened by urban growth and that excavation work should be carried out at the temple.
Live Science reached out to the team but did not hear back by the time of publication.

Some of the first people in North America lived through extreme climate change at the peak of the last ice age, a new study suggests.

Researchers studied ancient pollen locked in rocks at White Sands National Park in New Mexico, which houses an archaeological site thought to contain the oldest human footprints in the Americas. The researchers previously dated those footprints to around 21,000 to 23,000 years ago, though their age is the subject of some scientific debate because they are significantly older than other Indigenous sites in the Americas.

The new findings, published Wednesday (Oct. 14) in the journal Science Advances, suggest that humans kept using White Sands after temperatures warmed and thus saw the landscape undergo rapid changes during the coldest era of the last ice age, known as the Last Glacial Maximum (26,500 to 19,000 years ago).

"It's remarkable that early humans in the region were real-time witnesses to a rapidly changing environment discernible within a human lifetime — that is really food for thought," study co-author Kathleen Springer, a research geologist at the U.S. Geological Survey, said in a statement.

The White Sands footprints suggest that people from Asia reached the Americas via the region around the Bering Strait much earlier than scientists initially thought, challenging a long-held assumption that humans arrived on the continent around 13,000 years ago. While some scientists have disputed the methods used to date the footprints, evidence is building that they are around 23,000 years old.

White Sands contains footprints from various time periods, including footprints of a caregiver and a toddler who were there 10,000 years ago. Over thousands of years, people trudged across the New Mexico landscape alongside iconic ice age animals, including mammoths and giant ground sloths. The researchers have also discovered sled-like drag marks alongside ancient footprints at White Sands, providing evidence for a kind of travois — a wooden frame made from two poles bound together — that people likely would have used for transporting goods.

By looking at ancient pollen for the new study, researchers could deduce which plants grew across the millennia when humans lived in the area. The site's rock samples also contained waxes from plant leaves, membrane lipids from bacteria, and other organic molecules that helped the researchers better understand the environmental conditions of the time.

The analysis revealed that around 24,200 years ago, White Sands had a large lake and its surrounding mountains were coated in conifer trees (Pinus, Abies, and Picea). Then, over the next two millennia, temperatures rose, the lake began to shrink, and the conifer trees were replaced by oak trees (Quercus) and sagebrush, according to the statement.

"Throughout these periods of change, the people continued to visit and live in this area," study co-author Sally Reynolds, a paleoanthropologist at Bournemouth University in the U.K., said in the statement. "The sediments containing their footprints show us their environment changed significantly within individual human lifetimes."

The researchers speculated that people might have returned to White Sands at different times to benefit from the changing climate, with a shrinking lake potentially providing higher concentrations of animals and plants. However, while the footprints document that humans were present, they reveal little about their behavior.

"The footprints give us a snapshot of the people who lived there over 20,000 years ago," Reynolds said. "But they are not a continuous movie of their lives. They are individual frames — showing moments when humans, mud, water and chance came together."

What camera do most wildlife photographers use?

Dedicated wildlife photographers typically choose full-frame mirrorless cameras due to their larger sensor, better noise handling, accurate autofocus and rugged build. Many of these cameras also have fast burst rates, which is essential for capturing fast-moving wildlife or birds in flight.
Beginners and hobbyists can certainly get great shots with more portable models, but some compromises will have to be made in terms of speed and power.
What burst rate do I need for wildlife photography?

This depends on what kind of wildlife you're photographing, and how fast they move. Generally speaking, the best wildlife cameras have a burst rate of at least 20FPS (frames per second) — but the faster the better. If you photograph large, slow-moving mammals or stationary subjects, your burst rate doesn't need to be rattling off 40FPS at a time. If, however, you photograph birds in flight or fast moving animals, you will need a faster burst rate in order to capture that killer shot.
How many megapixels does a wildlife camera need?

There's no right or wrong answer here, but generally speaking, a higher resolution is preferred because it produces more detailed images, and you have more room to crop without losing image quality. However, more megapixels equals bigger file sizes, and you therefore need faster cards in order to keep up, especially when you're taking bursts.
That said, you can absolutely get some great shots with lower resolution cameras. We've been impressed by the quality of OM System cameras, and they typically only have around 20MP.
What is the best wildlife camera for beginners?

The most important aspect of a wildlife camera for beginners to prioritize is good autofocus. Provided your subject is in focus, you don't necessarily need the fastest burst rate, top of the line weather sealing or highest resolution.
For our money, Sony, Canon and Nikon offer the best autofocus on the market. We'd recommend the Sony A7C II, Canon EOS R7 or Nikon Zf for beginners.
How much should I spend on a wildlife camera?

You don't need to go overboard unless you're a professional wildlife photographer looking for the top of the range flagship models. You can get a really impressive wildlife camera for "most people" for anywhere between $2,000 and $3,000, but as many photographers will tell you, it's more beneficial to invest money in a better lens as opposed to splashing out on the very best camera.

Continuous improvement is a business strategy aimed at providing superior customer service through the implementation of a series of small changes in your operations and policies. These individual improvements may be centered around efficiency, productivity, employee happiness, or a multitude of other factors, but, ultimately, their purpose is to make your operation better at attracting, serving and retaining customers.

Continuous improvement is most closely associated with the Japanese word Kaizen. The post-World War II rebuilding of the Japanese industry led to several advances in manufacturing efficiency and quality control, many of which were the basis for “modern” manufacturing and business concepts like “lean” or “just-in-time” manufacturing, Six-Sigma quality control and improvement, and “The Toyota Way.” Each of these concepts has its own variation on identifying potential roadblocks to success, proposing solutions, implementing the means to those solutions, and analyzing the success or failure of any changes made.
Know your customer: by understanding the customer’s needs and wants, you can implement improvements that matter to them.
Let it flow: removing barriers to efficiency and reducing waste creates a smooth workflow.
Go to where the work happens: don’t manage from an office, see the problem firsthand.
Empower people: improvements and the resulting success require input from the “bottom up.”
Transparency: share plans, goals, and results with the entire team.

These principles can be applied to any problem in your operation, but continuous improvement is often used initially in smaller, incremental stages. These small changes are easier to implement, as they do not require a complete overhaul of company culture or the involvement of the entire staff. These can be “experimental” changes on a small scale, to test their effectiveness in specific situations or with a particular department. Breakthrough continuous improvements are larger in scale, and are most effective when a process or operation is in need of a complete overhaul. In either situation, proposed improvements should align with these five principles.

In order to transform the vague idea of a potential improvement into a clear plan of action with defined results, continuous improvement plans often rely on setting “SMART” goals. SMART is an acronym for “Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Timely.” SMART goals are a litmus test for determining if what you want to achieve is realistic and worthwhile to spend the time, energy, and money pursuing. Have you set a specific goal that accurately reflects the improvement(s) which you are hoping to implement? Can you measure the progress in a clear and meaningful way, so you know where you are in the process and know when you have achieved the goal? Is the improvement achievable with your current staff and resources? Are the changes relevant to your operation’s mission, values, and culture? And finally, is the goal time-sensitive? A goal without a deadline is more of a dream.

Once your organization has committed to continuous improvement and SMART goals have been set, the next step is to create and standardize the processes you want to use in working toward those goals. Staff must be given the tools (and the training) to implement any intended changes, and also an opportunity to express constructive opinions concerning the “real-world” effectiveness of the improvements. Project leaders should monitor the progress of each improvement project throughout the process and measure the results using key performance indicators (KPIs) tied to the results you hope to achieve through the planned changes.

If the process yields positive results, you are (as an organization) one step closer to achieving your goal of serving your customers more effectively. Share your successes with those who helped create them, with others in the organization who may benefit from the discovery, and, most importantly, with the customers whom you are doing this for in the first place!

In case you haven’t noticed, the parts business is a pretty crowded marketplace. In my own little hometown of less than 30,000 people, we have EIGHT parts stores! There are also eight OEM dealer franchises, so there is certainly no lack of options for purchasing auto parts and supplies in our area… and that doesn’t even include online options. With 16 places offering parts in the immediate area, if we want to make a sale we have to make our offerings more attractive than everyone else.

In order to stand out in a crowded market, your operation needs to add value to your products beyond whatever your competitors are offering. That “value” may take the form of different things to different consumers, but this sort of “it factor” is integral to making you stand out in a crowd. Since there are so many kinds of added value, identifying those things your customers value can be challenging.

The Value Stick may sound like some off-brand deodorant, but it’s a concept endorsed by Harvard Business School to visualize the four factors that help build a value-based business strategy. At the top of the stick is a customer’s “willingness to purchase” (WTP), and at the bottom lies your own “willingness to sell” (WTS). In between the two are your cost and the selling price of a product. These four markers are all, to some degree, moveable up or down The Value Stick. WTS primarily concerns the vendors who supply your parts and employees who provide labor for your store. It is the lowest price at which you can purchase your stock and pay someone to sell and distribute it to your customers. WTP, on the other hand, depends solely on a customer’s estimation of your product’s value, and represents the maximum amount of money they will hand over for your product at the point of sale.

Price can be a funny thing. For some, a higher price signals an increase in quality over a less-expensive product (brand name vs. generics, for example), or the cache of luxury (they’d pay $50 more for a Tommy Hilfiger shirt than a similar garment from Wal-Mart). For others, a higher price only means your business is making excessive profits… at their expense. (“I can buy the same thing on Amazon for $20 less than your price, why are you so high?”)

I believe that many of our customers (professional and amateur alike) still view the products we sell daily as interchangeable commodities. As parts professionals, we know better, but when we are faced with those customers for whom “any old thing will do,” we have to use other means to attract them to spend their money with us. Of the four variables along the Value Stick, WTP is the one we have the most influence over. Short of renegotiating supplier prices or reducing staffing costs, we don’t have much control over the cost of our inputs. We must maintain a reasonable margin in order to pay our overhead and keep ourselves in business, so deeply discounting prices is not a long-term solution. The only remaining way to move the needle is to increase the value of our product. Not the individual gasket, chassis part, or alternator, but rather through the experience of purchasing it from us.

All else being equal, people buy from the people and places they know and trust. It is easier to build these kinds of relationships with commercial customers simply because of the volume of their business. We have more opportunities to show them that we are an important partner in their success, and that we value that partnership. Prompt delivery, complete and accurate order fulfillment and ease of doing business are all value-added services that help justify a premium price tag. For the more occasional customer (professional or retail), we have a shorter window of opportunity to make a lasting impression. Superior customer service is still our greatest advantage with this sort of customer. Employing a knowledgeable and friendly staff, or even utilizing online lookup and ordering platforms can streamline the buying process for customers who value convenience.

Many retailers also build value into their product offering by providing additional services like code-reading, battery testing and installation, or loaner tool programs. Geared toward the non-professional segment of their customer base, these services also position the retailer as a trusted partner in maintaining personal vehicles. Adding value beyond the cost and quality of your parts increases retention and creates a scenario in which satisfied customers become advocates for your business. Give them something no one else can, and they have no reason to go anywhere else.

The battery thermal management system (BTMS) market is projected to grow from $5.26 billion in 2026 to $10.97 billion by 2033 at a CAGR of 11.1%, according to MarketsandMarkets. Increasing battery energy density, fast-charging requirements, higher power output, and stringent battery safety requirements are driving value and technology intensity in BTMS.

OEMs are transitioning from conventional air cooling toward liquid-cooled and integrated thermal architectures to manage battery temperature with greater precision and efficiency. Technology is also shifting toward AI-based thermal simulation, cell-level temperature monitoring, direct cell cooling, and intelligent controls, particularly for high-voltage 800V EV platforms requiring faster charging and tighter thermal uniformity. 800V BTMS solutions are being developed with higher coolant flow, faster preconditioning, and integrated battery heating and cooling to manage higher charging loads, according to the MarketsandMarkets report.
MAHLE Expands Battery Cooling Plate Production in Spain

In June 2026, MAHLE started series production of battery cooling plates at its Montblanc plant in Spain to support growing demand for liquid-cooled battery systems. The company plans to increase production from around 1,000 units per week to 8,000 units per week by the end of 2026, with the facility capable of reaching up to 15,000 units per week.

The cooling plates use optimized coolant channels to distribute heat uniformly across the battery and maintain operating temperatures below 40°C. MAHLE is also expanding the production area by around 10,000 m², supporting higher-volume production of battery thermal management components.
Webasto Develops Heated Chiller for Integrated Thermal Management

In December 2025, Webasto developed its Heated Chiller to combine battery cooling, battery heating, and cabin heating within a single thermal management unit. The system integrates the chiller, battery heater, and interior heater, reducing component count and simplifying thermal system integration.

The architecture supports coordinated temperature control across the battery and cabin, enabling battery preconditioning for charging while also meeting cabin heating requirements. Webasto is positioning the Heated Chiller as a compact thermal management solution for electric vehicles, with the technology progressing toward production applications.
BEV Segment Expected to Lead Global BTMS Market

The BEV segment is expected to have the largest share in the global BTMS market. BEVs are expected to be the fastest-growing vehicle type, as they account for more than 50% globally, supported by higher battery energy density, tighter cell temperature-control requirements, and greater integration of battery and vehicle thermal systems.

Within passenger BEVs, NMC batteries require active thermal control as higher energy density and charging power increase heat generation and cell temperature variation. This supports liquid cooling, direct cell cooling, battery preconditioning, and active temperature control. OEMs and BTMS suppliers are focusing on integrated and actively controlled thermal architectures.

For instance, the Mercedes AMG GT 4-Door Coupe uses direct cooling of cylindrical NCMA battery cells, with intelligent thermal management controlling cell temperature during high-power operation, while Bosch provides intelligent battery temperature control and diagnostics for BEVs.

These developments are increasing the need for optimized coolant distribution, low-thermal-resistance cooling structures, and coordinated thermal control across the battery, heat pump, HVAC, electric motor, and power electronics. High energy density batteries and higher charging power are supporting demand for advanced active BTMS solutions, particularly for NMC-based passenger BEVs.

This episode of DriveTime features Matt Buchholz, CEO of MotoRad. In this interview, Buchholz described how the company’s D.R.I.V.E. core values — Dedication, Relationship, Innovation, Value Driven and Expertise — provide the cultural foundation for how its team operates internally and engages with customers and channel partners.

Buchholz emphasized that culture and strategy are closely connected. As MotoRad expands across thermal management, emissions and powertrain controls, Buchholz said investment decisions begin with market intelligence and listening directly to customers. The company looks for opportunities that fit its existing capabilities and strategy while addressing clear market needs. Buchholz said it also evaluates adjacent categories for “low friction” opportunities where it can create value quickly. In many cases, some of MotoRad’s strongest product ideas have originated with technicians, counter professionals and other customers who identify ways the company can improve a product or make a repair easier.

Looking ahead, Buchholz said MotoRad’s growth strategy centers on three areas: commercial execution, operational agility and technology. Commercially, the company plans to continue listening to the market, responding faster and creating greater value through areas such as coverage, service, business intelligence and quality. Operationally, MotoRad is focused on diversifying its global supply chain to maintain continuity of supply and become nimbler. Technology supports both priorities by improving efficiency, reducing waste and helping the company respond to rapidly increasing expectations for speed.

Buchholz also sees continued opportunity for the broader aftermarket as vehicle miles traveled and vehicle age increase and vehicle technologies across thermal management, emissions and powertrain controls become more complex. “We get to support this incredibly essential business that people enjoy,” he said.

Ever drive a vehicle that just doesn’t feel right anymore? Maybe it wanders down the highway. Maybe there’s a clunk every time you hit a pothole. Maybe the steering wheel isn’t centered, the tires are wearing unevenly, or it just doesn’t inspire the confidence it used to.

The truth is, steering and suspension problems rarely come from a single worn out part. Every control arm, ball joint, tie rod, sway bar link, and bushing work together as one connected system. When one connection starts to wear, it puts added stress on the rest of the system, and before long, that small problem becomes several bigger ones.
That system level approach is exactly how TrakMotive has positioned its Suspensia brand chassis program. Learn more about it in this video, sponsored by TrakMotive.

The third generation of the Toyota RAV4 shares all of the same infrastructure with the Corolla and many other Toyota vehicles. The front suspension is easy to adjust, while the rear needs a little more attention.

If you get one in your shop, it’s what you do after you adjust the angles that can make or break the alignment. The RAV4 has electric power steering and the stability control is a very common option. These systems need to know the correct steering angle to operate. If it is not reset, it could result in the customer coming back with the VSA or steering malfunction indicator light on.

Always pay attention to the ride height. If the springs are weak, it can change the camber and caster in the front. In the rear, weak springs can change the camber and toe and cause the inner edges of the tires to wear prematurely. Often many of the alignment angles can be corrected with new springs or loaded struts.

The front suspension on the RAV4 uses a MacPherson strut design. Caster is not adjustable from the factory. Camber can be adjusted using additional parts. Toyota uses coded bolts with dots on the heads that indicate a fixed range of camber. But, the aftermarket has a better solution, with cam bolts that can adjust ±1.75 degrees.

The most common wear points for the RAV4 are the lower control arms. The bushings on the arm can degrade and cause changes in the caster, camber and toe. Changing the control arm involves removing the lower crossmember.

The rear suspension is a multilink design. On high-mileage vehicles, inspect the lower knuckle bushing for play and deflection. Another sign of a worn bushing is premature tire wear on the inside edge of the rear tires.

The rear toe links use a sleeve that connects the two portions of the rod. The sleeves are problematic. The sleeves and jam nuts can come loose if you don’t take your time using the correct procedures. Don’t try to tighten both jam nuts at the same time. Instead, grab the sleeve with a crow’s foot and torque wrench and put an open-end wrench on the jam nuts. Tighten the sleeve to 15 ft/lbs.

If you get a 2005-2011 Toyota RAV4 in your shop for an alignment with a complaint of either rear tire wear or a knocking noise, you need to be aware of a recall and inspection campaign Toyota issued in 2012. Toyota Safety Recall COJ involved inspecting the right and left toe links for looseness. Based upon this inspection, it may have been necessary to replace the arm(s).

Toyota received reports from dealers indicating that some vehicles experienced symptoms of the recalled condition after being inspected or repaired. Toyota discovered that some inspections were not up to standards.

If a lower toe link was inspected and has passed, it will have an epoxy and plastic covering indicating that it passed the inspection. The bad news is that if the cover is there, the toe can’t be adjusted and must be replaced. There are aftermarket toe links that utilize a better design than the original Toyota part.

Camber can be adjusted with an adjustable upper arm. These arms can give an additional three degrees of adjustment. These components can give adjustments for the rest of the life of the vehicle and allow for fine-tuning of the rear camber angles to maximize tire life.

Most 2006-2013 RAV4 models are equipped with an optional Vehicle Stability Control (VSC) system that requires a scan tool and special procedures to perform a zero-point calibration of the steering angle sensor. It is highly recommended to do this through the OBD-II port with a scan tool. Yes, it is possible to reset the system by jumping two pins in the diagnostic connector and disconnecting the battery. But, there is no way to confirm or document the calibration was properly performed.

The steering position sensor’s basic function is to monitor the driver’s steering inputs. This includes the angle of the steering wheel and/or the rate at which the driver is turning the wheel. The steering position sensor on the RAV4 is located behind the steering wheel and is a high-resolution sensor.

The VSC system relies on accurate steering input from the steering angle sensor to analyze a situation and apply appropriate measures to help direct the vehicle on the intended path. If the system is not calibrated after a toe adjustment, the system will not operate properly and may illuminate the VSC malfunction light after the driver has picked up their RAV4.
The Toyota VSC system uses the information from the steering position sensor and compares the information to the yaw rate sensor to determine what the car is doing.

When a vehicle is aligned and the toe in the front or rear is altered, it changes the thrust angle of the vehicle. The thrust angle is directly connected with the slip angle and the measurements taken by the yaw position sensor. Even if you adjust only the rear toe, you are altering the thrust angle, and the steering position sensor must be recalibrated.

After the sensor is reset, it is necessary to drive the vehicle and turn the steering wheel to the right and left at the speed of 22 mph (35 km/h) for at least five seconds to calibrate the sensors and complete the reset. If this is not performed, the VSC may set a code and the sensor may read 1150 degrees. This is not an indication the sensor is faulty, only that it has not been properly reset.
The quarter tire test can provide an earlier warning of tire wear than the traditional penny test. The penny test checks for about 2/32˝ of tread, while a quarter checks closer to 4/32˝.
The 2/32˝ measurement represents the minimum replacement point. Checking at 4/32˝ gives drivers more time to plan for tire replacement.

Insert a quarter into the tire tread with Washington’s head facing down. If the top of Washington’s head disappears, the tire has at least 4/32˝ of tread. If the top of his head remains visible, drivers can begin planning for replacement.

In wet-weather testing, tires worn to 4/32˝ took an average of 87 feet longer to stop than new tires. Wet performance can therefore decline before tread reaches the level measured by the penny test. The quarter test provides an earlier indication of tread wear.
A new report from Volvo finds that equal protection for men and women can be achieved through data-driven safety development grounded in real-world crash research, the release states.
The research found that overall injury for drivers has decreased by 79% for Volvo models from 2010 to 2019 compared to models from 1970 to 1979.
Volvo saw an 88% decrease for women, bringing the injury risk to the same level as men, the release states.

“The results also show substantial advances in occupant protection across all seating positions,” the release adds. “Restrained rear-seat occupants in Volvo cars benefit from protection levels comparable to, and in some cases exceeding, those of front-seat occupants.”

Volvo says the data underscores the effectiveness of decades of rear-seat safety innovation in Volvo cars. This happened with the lack of regulatory requirements and standardized testing, the release states.

“For too long, safety in the automotive industry has not worked equally well for everyone,” says Åsa Haglund, Volvo head of Cars Safety Centre, in the release. “At Volvo Cars, we’ve taken a different approach. By studying real-world crashes and designing with the needs of women, men and children of all body types in mind, we’ve worked for decades to provide a high level of protection regardless of who you are or where you sit in the car. Our latest research confirms that equal protection is not just an ambition, but something we have been able to achieve in Volvo cars for many years.”

Volvo has collected data since 1970 from more than 50,000 real-world crashes involving more than 80,000 occupants, the release notes. It adds that the insights are translated into safety requirements, testing, vehicle development, verification, and production.
“The result is a continuous cycle of learning that helps drive innovations and improve protection for everyone,” according to the release.
The study also reviewed different crash types. It found that frontal impact injuries were reduced by 79% for all drivers. Side impacts saw a larger reduction in injuries at 89%.

The approach also laid the foundation for pioneering Volvo Cars Safety Standard, according to the release. Through the standard, Volvo sets its own benchmark for real-world safety, going beyond regulation or safety ratings, Volvo says.

“And because real-world crashes don’t involve standardized crash test dummies, Volvo Cars’ research involves considering a diverse range of occupant characteristics, including gender, height, body shape and weight,” the release states. “As a result, the company’s safety innovations are designed with the same diversity in mind.”

Volvo notes it has openly shared its safety research to help raise safety standards across the industry through the Equal Vehicles for All (E.V.A.) initiative launched in 2019. It adds that more than 50 years of safety research is freely accessible in a digital library. Carmakers, researchers and policyholders can use the data to build on Volvo’s insights.

The recent study focuses on a broad range of real-world crash scenarios, including frontal, side, and rear-end impacts; run-off-road collisions; rollovers; side-swipe collisions; large animal impacts; and multi-collision crashes.

It also focuses on belted occupants aged 13 or older and examines injuries with moderate potential to threaten life, such as fractures and concussions, while excluding minor injuries such as bruises and pain.

The Volvo EX60 was the first vehicle equipped with the multi-adaptive seatbelt.
